Why watch?
If this is your first view—hi, I’m Nick! TLDR: I spent six years building automated businesses with Make.com (most notably 1SecondCopy, a content company that hit 7 figures). Today a lot of people talk about automation, but I’ve noticed that very few have practical, real world success making money with it. So this channel is me chiming in and showing you what *real* systems that make *real* revenue look like.

Hopefully I can help you improve your business, and in doing so, the rest of your life 🙏

Like, subscribe, and leave me a comment if you have a specific request! Thanks.

metadata.title: Turn Your AI Skills Into Long-Term Clients (The 90-Day Method)
metadata.author: Jeff Sauer - Service Stacking
metadata.shortDescription:
You can't just ask an AI client for a retainer. Nobody pays every month because you asked. In this video I break down the two kinds of AI clients I work with: the DIYer who needs a muse for a few months and then moves on, and the client who wants AI working in their business but doesn't want to push the buttons. The second kind stays, and I'll show you how the first ninety days turn them into a long-term client.

You'll learn what to call the ongoing role (I call it an AI Enablement Partner), why "a fee for availability" loses to "a fee with accountability," what a short monthly update does for retention, and what this work is worth: two thousand to fifteen thousand dollars a month per client.

Which kind of AI client do you mostly have, the DIYer or the one who wants a partner? Tell me in the comments.

═══════════════════════════════════════

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:

00:00 - Two buckets of AI clients
00:47 - Who I am and why I work this way
01:24 - Why pitching a retainer fails
02:32 - The DIYer vs the client who stays
04:07 - Free newsletter: AI-First Business
04:21 - The AI Enablement Partner
05:03 - What people get wrong (the ninety days)
05:46 - Which kind of client do you have?
05:56 - Why they keep paying: the monthly update
07:26 - What it pays: $2K to $15K a month
07:54 - What you do now becomes what you're known for
08:28 - Wrap-up

═══════════════════════════════════════

RESOURCES MENTIONED:

📬 AI-First Business, my free newsletter on building an AI-first service business:
→ https://profitschool.com/newsletter

🎓 Want help building your AI service business? MeasureU Pro:
→ https://measureu.com/pro

Tools & Platforms Referenced:
→ Claude Code (Anthropic)
→ OpenAI Codex
→ Grok (xAI)
→ CRM, dashboards and conversion rate optimization (the client example)

═══════════════════════════════════════

MORE AI SERVICE BUSINESS VIDEOS:

→ Stop Selling Hours: Become the AI Consultant Clients Retain
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hhTBH0qUDH4

→ How to Sell AI Agents to Clients Who Don't Know What AI Is
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ajpbZfYWIew

→ Become a One-Person Agency With AI
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=307DiVtiBzE

→ Your Client's GA4 Conversion Rate Is Wrong (Here's the Fix)
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RuHkSZ7mLBE

═══════════════════════════════════════

ABOUT THIS CHANNEL:

I'm Jeff Sauer. I've spent 20+ years in analytics and digital marketing, built and exited an 8-figure agency, and trained over 3,000 marketers through MeasureU. This channel is about service stacking: building a solo or small-agency business with AI. I break down what to sell, how to price it, and how to keep clients when the tools change every month.

Subscribe for more: https://www.youtube.com/@jeffalytics?sub_confirmation=1

CONNECT:

metadata.title: Zapier vs Make vs n8n: Which Costs Less for Small Businesses? (2026)
metadata.author: AI Business Tools & Automation
metadata.shortDescription:
Zapier vs Make vs n8n: which automation tool fits your business? We take one lead follow-up workflow (1 trigger + 5 actions, 500 leads a month) and price it in all three using each company's official pricing page. You'll learn what each tool actually counts (tasks, credits or executions), where each one is strongest, and how to test before you buy. The workflow costs in the video are illustrative calculations, not quotes.

Chapters
0:00 Same workflow, three bills
0:19 The test workflow
0:57 Tasks vs credits vs executions
1:20 Zapier
2:55 Make
4:25 n8n
6:00 Which one should you choose?
6:51 How to test before you buy + what's next

Prices checked Nov 4, 2026; check the live pages, because plans and prices change.
- Zapier Professional (billed annually): $19.99/mo for 750 tasks, $49/mo for 2,000 tasks, $89/mo for 5,000 tasks. AI steps can use more tasks depending on model tier; see the task-rate page.
- Make: prices are region-dependent and vary by country, so we don't quote an official number. Check the price shown on the pricing page or in your account. (Figures mentioned in the video are from Make's comparison page and an independent reviewer, labeled as such.)
- n8n cloud (billed annually): Starter €20/mo for 2.5K executions, Pro €50/mo for 10K executions. n8n's self-hostable Community Edition is under the Sustainable Use License (fair-code), which has limits on commercial use and redistribution; enterprise features need a separate paid license.

Official pricing pages
Zapier: https://zapier.com/pricing
Zapier task rates: https://zapier.com/pricing/rates
Make: https://www.make.com/en/pricing
n8n: https://n8n.io/pricing/
n8n license: https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/master/LICENSE.md

Not sponsored. No affiliate links. This video is not financial or purchasing advice; run one real workflow on each free tier or trial for a week and read the usage meter before you commit.

Next video: building this exact lead follow-up workflow in n8n, with a human approval step before any AI-drafted email goes out.

Related channels worth watching: @KevinStratvert, @nateherk and @NetworkChuck #Qazi
#n8n #Zapier #MakeCom #NoCode #AIAutomation #WorkflowAutomation #SmallBusiness #ZapierVsMake

Most remote teams don't have a tool problem. They have a time problem. The more tools you use, the more time that gets wasted moving information between them. metadata.title: I Run My AI Automation Business for $0 in Software (Zapier vs Make vs n8n)
metadata.author: Jonas | AI Tools & Automation
metadata.shortDescription:
I run 100+ real automations for clients and the software itself costs me $0. In this video I break down the 4 ways to actually build (and sell) AI automations — Zapier, Make, n8n Cloud, and self-hosted n8n — how each one really charges you (tasks vs credits vs executions), and the exact free setup I run myself.

What I cover:
• What an automation actually is (trigger + actions)
• Hosted vs self-hosted tools, and why self-hosted can be free
• Zapier: free plan, $19.99/mo Pro, 9,000+ apps, how task pricing can bite you
• Make: visual canvas, 1,000 free credits/mo
• n8n: AI agent steps, Cloud pricing (20€/mo and 50€/mo) vs the free self-hosted community edition on a ~€6/mo VPS
• A real look inside my own n8n: 100+ workflows for WhatsApp bots, payment syncs and lead follow-ups
• Which tool to start on if you've never built an automation
• 5 rules I follow so client automations don't break quietly
• 5 things businesses actually pay for

Tools mentioned:
Zapier: https://zapier.com
Make: https://make.com
n8n: https://n8n.io
Hostinger (what I host my own n8n on): https://hostinger.com
PhotoCraft (free, open-source Photoshop alternative): https://photocraft.im

Chapters
0:00 Intro: free AI tools that copy paid software
1:01 4 ways to build an automation business
1:13 What is an automation (trigger + actions)
1:43 Hosted vs self-hosted tools
2:03 How platforms charge you (tasks/credits/executions)
2:34 Zapier breakdown
3:09 Make breakdown
3:44 n8n breakdown + my own setup
6:11 Which tool should you use
6:39 5 rules for client automations
7:54 5 things businesses pay for
9:04 Outro + free resources

#automation #n8n #AItools

metadata.title: Zapier vs Make vs n8n: What One AI Workflow Really Costs (2026 Pricing)
metadata.author: ProfitPilot
metadata.shortDescription:
One AI lead-handling workflow (website form → AI summary & tag → Google Sheets → Gmail reply → Slack alert), priced on Zapier, Make, and n8n at 100, 500, and 2,000 leads a month — based on each tool's published pricing, not a sponsored test.

Chapters
0:00 Same workflow, different bills
0:42 How each tool bills
1:46 The workflow we're pricing
2:47 Costs at 100, 500, 2,000 leads
4:18 The AI tier multiplier
5:52 Verdict + price your own

Key numbers (annual billing): at 500 leads/mo, Zapier Pro $49 (2,000 tasks, Standard AI tier) or $89 if the AI step stays on Premium, which Zapier's help center says is the default for new AI steps on paid plans; Make Core $9 (as listed on Make's own pages; make.com/pricing blocks automated checks); n8n Cloud Starter €20 (2,500 executions). Task/credit counts are our calculation from published rules (worst case: every step runs), not a measured test. AI model/API costs not included.

Prices checked Oct 29, 2026. Annual-billing prices; Zapier and Make in USD, n8n in EUR as listed (not converted). Prices change often — check the official pages before buying.

Sources (official):
• Zapier pricing: https://zapier.com/pricing
• Zapier – How task usage is measured: https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/8496196837261
• Zapier – AI by Zapier model tier pricing: https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/46425475442829
• Make pricing: https://www.make.com/en/pricing
• Make – Make vs Zapier (lists Core at $9/mo for 10,000 credits): https://www.make.com/en/compare/make-vs-zapier
• Make Help – Extra credits: https://help.make.com/extra-credits

Disclosure: the narration voice in this video is synthetic (AI-generated text-to-speech, Piper 'ljspeech' voice). Graphics are illustrations generated from published pricing; no app screenshots. Not sponsored; no affiliate links.

segments.text: Same workflow.
Very different bills.
Here's what one small-business automation costs on Zapier,
Make, and n8n, based on each tool's published pricing,
checked on October 29, 2026.
One workflow, three volumes, three price tags.
And one Zapier setting that quietly changes the bill.
Quick note: this video isn't sponsored, and there are no affiliate links.
All prices are for annual billing.
Zapier and Make prices are in US dollars.
n8n showed its plans in euros when we checked, so that's what we use,
with no currency conversion.
First, the key to everything: each tool counts something different.
Zapier bills in tasks.
A task is an action step that runs successfully.
Triggers don't count, and neither do built-in tools like Filter,
Paths, and Formatter.
Make bills in credits.
Most modules use one credit each time they run,
and that includes the trigger.
Routers and error handlers don't use credits.
n8n bills in executions.
One execution is one full run of a workflow, no matter how many steps it has.
So when you add a step, Zapier and Make cost more per run.
n8n doesn't.
And when you run out?
Zapier can switch you to pay-per-task at a higher rate,
up to a cap, or hold your runs until the next billing cycle.
With Make, scenarios stop until you add credits,
and extra credits cost 25% more than the credits in your plan.
n8n's Starter and Pro plans are capped, with no overage fees.
Here's the workflow we're pricing.
It's a common one: AI lead handling.
A lead fills out a form on your website.
An AI step summarizes the request and tags it hot,
warm, or cold.
The lead is added to Google Sheets, gets a reply email from Gmail,
and your team gets a Slack alert.
That's one trigger and four actions.
On Zapier, the trigger is free and each action is one task,
if the AI step uses the Standard model tier.
So, four tasks per run.
On Make, all five modules count, including the trigger.
That's about five credits per run, assuming the AI module uses your own OpenAI
connection and bills like a normal module.
On n8n, it's one execution per run, whether the workflow has five steps or fifty.
These counts assume every step runs every time.
That's a worst case, and it's our calculation from the published rules,
not a measured test.
Now the costs, at three volumes.
At 100 leads a month, Zapier needs 400 tasks.
The free plan only allows two-step Zaps, so it's the smallest Pro tier,
at $19.99 a month.
Make needs about 500 credits, which fits inside the free plan's 1,000 monthly
credits.
n8n Cloud has no free plan, so it's Starter, at €20.
At 500 leads, Zapier needs 2,000 tasks, which is the $49 tier.
Make needs about 2,500 credits, so the Core plan, at $9.
n8n is still Starter, at €20, because Starter includes 2,500 executions.
At 2,000 leads, Zapier needs 8,000 tasks, so the 10,000-task tier,
Make needs about 10,000 credits.
That's exactly Core's limit, with no headroom, so expect to buy extra credits or
move up a tier.
n8n is 2,000 executions, still inside Starter.
So in this example, Make had the lowest price at all three volumes,
n8n stayed flat, and Zapier climbed with every lead.
One note on Make: its pricing page blocks automated checks,
so we're quoting what Make's own pages list: Core at $9 a month for 10,000 credits.
Check the live page before you buy.
Now, that setting I mentioned: the AI model tier.
AI by Zapier steps come in three tiers.
Standard costs one task, Advanced costs three, and Premium costs five.
If the AI calls tools, each tool call is billed at the same rate.
And here's the catch: Zapier's help center says new AI by Zapier steps on paid plans
default to Premium.
So unless you change it, our AI step costs five tasks,
not one.
Every run becomes eight tasks instead of four.
That moves the bill from $19.99 to $39 at 100 leads,
from $49 to $89 at 500, and from $129 to $189 at 2,000.
Same workflow.
Same leads.
One dropdown.
And if a Premium AI step also calls two tools, that single step uses 15 tasks per run.
Should you always pick Standard?
Not necessarily.
A simple summarize-and-tag job may work fine on Standard,
but test the output before you switch.
On Make, Make's own pages say features that use AI may consume more than one credit.
With your own OpenAI key, OpenAI also bills you for tokens.
On n8n, an AI node doesn't change the count.
It's still one execution per run.
And none of these numbers include what the AI model itself costs.
So, who should pick which?
Zapier, if you want the most guided setup.
Even Make's comparison page calls Zapier's step-by-step interface genuinely
beginner-friendly.
Just check the AI tier on every AI step.
Make, if you want the lowest price at these volumes,
and you're fine with a visual builder that takes longer to learn.
n8n Cloud, if your workflows are long or built around AI,
because extra steps don't add to the bill.
And self-hosted n8n is free, but n8n's docs say it takes technical expertise,
and maintenance is your responsibility.
Features like workflow and credential sharing still need a paid license.
To price your own workflow, start with your runs per month.
For Zapier, count the action steps that actually run,
and check the AI tier.
For Make, count every module, including the trigger.
For n8n, your runs are your executions.
Then pick the smallest plan that leaves some headroom.
Prices were checked on October 29, 2026.
They change often, so use the official links in the description before you buy.
Subscribe to ProfitPilot for a new, no-hype breakdown of AI and automation tools
every week.

Welcome to Everyday AI Automation!

💡 Learn simple AI tools, automations, and time-saving workflows — no tech experience required.

▶️ Recommended videos:
https://youtu.be/rGOHj2S5Zq8?si=oKRIltWoUXiTVhCh

🔧 Tools mentioned in this video:

⚡ Zapier
https://zapier.com/

🔵 Make

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔗 OTHER TOOLS USED IN THE EXAMPLES

📧 Gmail
https://mail.google.com/

📊 Google Sheets
https://sheets.google.com/

🧠 OpenAI / ChatGPT
https://openai.com/

📄 UiPath Document Understanding
https://www.uipath.com/product/document-understanding

📩 FREE AI Automation Starter Kit:
https://everydayaiautomation.lovable.app/

📘 Connect with me:

💼 LinkedIn  
https://www.linkedin.com/in/thomas-pyatt/

𝕏 
https://x.com/ThomasPyatt14

📸 Instagram  
https://www.instagram.com/thomaspyatt/

📘 Facebook  
https://www.facebook.com/thomas.pyatt.16


Zapier, Make, n8n, and UiPath all automate work — but they don't automate work in exactly the same way.

So which automation platform should YOU learn? 🤔

In this video, we're breaking down four of the biggest automation platforms and looking at what each one actually does, where it shines, its limitations, and the types of workflows it's best suited for.

This isn't about declaring one platform the winner.

It's about understanding how automation works and choosing the right tool for the job.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔥 IN THIS VIDEO

⚡ ZAPIER

Learn why Zapier is one of the easiest ways to get started with automation and how triggers and actions can connect applications like Gmail and Google Sheets.

🔵 MAKE

See how Make approaches automation visually and why its scenarios, filters, routers, and multi-step workflows give you more flexibility as your automations grow.

⚙️ n8n

Discover why n8n has become increasingly popular for AI automation, APIs, complex logic, branching, data manipulation, and workflows requiring deeper control.

🤖 UIPATH

Learn how Robotic Process Automation (RPA) differs from traditional app-to-app automation and how UiPath can automate repetitive work involving documents, browsers, business applications, clicking, typing, and data entry.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧠 WHICH ONE SHOULD YOU LEARN?

If you're completely new to automation:
➡️ Start by exploring Zapier.

If you want visual, multi-step workflows:
➡️ Take a look at Make.

If you want deeper control, APIs, AI, logic, and more complex workflows:
➡️ Explore n8n.

If you need to automate repetitive work inside documents, browsers, desktop applications, or enterprise systems:
➡️ Look at UiPath.

But the most important skill isn't memorizing one automation platform.

It's learning how to look at a business process and ask:

What triggers the process?

What information needs to move?

What decisions need to happen?

Where is repetitive manual work happening?

Where could AI add value?

Where should a human remain involved?

And which technology is best suited to solve the problem?

That's automation literacy.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎬 WANT THE STEP-BY-STEP TUTORIALS?

I've built real workflows using these platforms on Everyday AI Automation.

⚡ Zapier:
How to Automatically Save Gmail Leads to Google Sheets With Zapier
https://youtu.be/T0nt5dNR-0M

🔵 Make:
Build an AI Email Assistant With Make + ChatGPT — Step by Step
https://youtu.be/PGVQJZbcpbg

⚙️ n8n:
Build an AI Lead Automation With n8n — Step by Step
https://youtu.be/rGOHj2S5Zq8

🤖 UiPath:
Automate Invoice Data Entry With UiPath — Step by Step
https://youtu.be/XHBHodnaLkU

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💬 YOUR TURN

If you could learn ONE of these automation platforms next, which would you choose?

⚡ Zapier
🔵 Make
⚙️ n8n
🤖 UiPath

Tell me which one — and WHY — in the comments.

If there's another automation platform you think I should test, tell me that too. Your suggestion might become a future Everyday AI Automation video.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

If you found this comparison useful, hit LIKE and SUBSCRIBE for practical AI tools, real automation workflows, honest reviews, and step-by-step tutorials.

No magic.
No overnight promises.

Practical AI. No Hype.

#Zapier #Make #n8n #UiPath #AIAutomation #Automation #RPA #WorkflowAutomation #NoCode #EverydayAIAutomation

metadata.title: n8n vs Zapier vs Make (2026): Which AI Automation Tool Is Actually Worth It?
metadata.author: Whizz AI
metadata.shortDescription:
n8n vs Zapier vs Make in 2026 — which AI automation tool is actually worth it for your business?

In this video I compare all three with real prices, real limits, and a clear answer for each type of business. No hype, just the facts that change the decision.

What you will learn:
- How AI changed automation in 2026
- Zapier: easiest to start, 9,000+ apps, Professional from $19.99/month
- Make: visual builder, Core from $9/month billed annually for 10,000 credits
- n8n: self-host free with the Community Edition, Starter 20 euros/month billed annually
- A real workflow that works on all three: Gmail to AI summary to Google Sheets to Slack
- Which tool to choose if you are a beginner, a small business, or a technical builder

Prices were checked on 14 November 2026 from the official pricing pages. Prices can change, so check the links below for the latest price before you buy.

Official pricing pages:
Zapier: https://zapier.com/pricing
Make: https://www.make.com/en/pricing
n8n: https://n8n.io/pricing/

Chapters:
0:00 The question
0:07 What changed in 2026
1:05 Zapier
2:33 Make
4:00 n8n
5:27 Side by side and a real workflow
6:55 Verdict: which one should you choose?
7:49 Next video

Next video: I will build that email workflow step by step in n8n, with no code.

This video is for education and comparison. It is not sponsored by Zapier, Make, or n8n.

segments.text: You are probably paying too much for automation, or building it the hard way. In this video, I compare n8n, Zapier, and Make in 2026, with real prices, real limits, and one clear answer for each type of business. No hype, just the facts that change the decision.
Automation used to be simple. If this happens, do that. A new email arrives, you get a notification. A form is filled in, a row appears in a spreadsheet. That was useful, but it was limited.

In 2026, the change is AI inside the workflow. These tools can now read an email, decide what it means, draft a reply, summarise a document, and ask you to approve it before anything goes out. The workflow is no longer just moving data. It is making a small decision, and then acting on it.

So here is how I judged them. First, how easy is it to start, if you do not write code. Second, what does it really cost when you use it every day. Third, how well does AI work inside it. And fourth, how much control do you have.
Let us start with Zapier, because it is the one most people have heard of.

Zapier is the easiest of the three to start with. You pick a trigger, like a new email in Gmail, and then you pick an action, like creating a row in Google Sheets, or sending a message in Slack. You do not need to write code. The editor is simple, and the steps are clear.

Zapier also connects to more apps than the others. On its own pricing page, Zapier says it connects to more than 9,000 apps. That matters when you use a niche tool, because the chances are high that Zapier already supports it.
Zapier now includes AI steps, tables, and forms, so it is becoming a full platform, not just a simple connector.

Now the price. Zapier has a free plan at zero dollars a month, with 100 tasks a month. A task is counted when Zapier successfully completes an action. The Professional plan starts from 19 dollars and 99 cents a month. That plan adds multi-step workflows, unlimited premium apps, webhooks, and AI fields. The Team plan starts from 69 dollars a month, and adds shared workspaces and up to 25 users. New accounts also get a 14-day free trial of the Professional plan, with no credit card required.

So what is the catch? Cost as you grow. Every successful action counts as a task, and AI steps and external calls can use more than one. If you run a lot of small automations every day, your task count climbs fast, and so does your bill. Zapier is simple and powerful, but it is the most expensive of the three at scale.
Pick Zapier if you want the easiest start, the widest choice of apps, and you are happy to pay for that convenience.
Next is Make, which used to be called Integromat.

Make is visual in a different way. Instead of a list of steps, you draw your workflow on a canvas. You can see branches, filters, and routers, all on one screen. For a complex workflow, that picture makes it much easier to understand what is happening, and where it can go wrong.

Make charges in credits, not tasks. Since August 2025, Make calls its billing unit a credit. In most cases, every module that runs in a scenario uses one credit. A scenario is Make's name for a workflow. So if your scenario has five modules, and it runs 100 times, that is about 500 credits.

Make has a free plan with 1,000 credits a month. Its Core plan is listed from 9 dollars a month, billed annually, for 10,000 credits, with unlimited active scenarios and scheduling down to one minute. That is a lot of capacity for the price, which is why Make is often the cheapest option for a small business.

Make also says it offers integrations with more than 1,000 third-party apps. That is far fewer than Zapier, but it still covers the popular tools most businesses use, like Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, and Airtable.
The catch with Make is that the price depends on how many modules you use. A long scenario costs more on every run, because every module counts.
Pick Make if you want a visual builder, a low monthly cost, and you are building workflows with several steps that run often.
Now n8n, the tool that has grown fastest with technical users and AI builders.

n8n is different because you can run it yourself. There is a free Community Edition that you can self-host on your own server, available on GitHub. That means your data stays with you, and you are not paying per step in the same way. For many businesses, that control matters, especially when workflows handle customer data.
n8n is also built for AI agents. You can build workflows where an AI agent uses tools, reads data, and takes actions across your apps, with code when you need it and no-code steps when you do not.

The hosted pricing is clear. The Starter plan is 20 euros a month, billed annually, and it is hosted by n8n. The Pro plan is 50 euros a month, billed annually, for solo builders and small teams running automations in production. The Business plan is 667 euros a month, billed annually. n8n also says, unlike other tools that charge per step or user, you only pay when a workflow runs from start to finish.

So what is the catch? n8n is harder to start with. The interface is powerful, but it is not as friendly as Zapier for a complete beginner. And if you self-host the free version, you are responsible for keeping it running, updating it, and securing it. That is a real job, even if the software itself costs nothing.
Pick n8n if you want control, you want to build AI agents, you are comfortable with a little technical setup, or you want to avoid paying per step as you grow.
Let us put them side by side, so the choice is simple.
For ease of use, Zapier wins. It is the simplest to learn, and the fastest to set up.
For visual building and low cost, Make wins. Its canvas makes complex work clear, and its Core plan gives you 10,000 credits for 9 dollars a month, billed annually.
For control and AI agents, n8n wins. You can self-host it for free, and you are not charged per step in the same way.
For the widest choice of apps, Zapier wins, with more than 9,000 apps. Make covers more than 1,000 apps, which is enough for most businesses.
Now, here is one workflow that works on all three, and it shows what modern automation actually looks like.

A new enquiry email arrives in Gmail. The workflow reads it, uses AI to summarise what the customer wants, and checks whether it is a sales enquiry, a support question, or something else. It adds a row to Google Sheets, with the customer name, the summary, and the category. Then it sends a short message to your team in Slack, so someone can reply quickly.

On Zapier, that is a Zap with a Gmail trigger, an AI step, a Sheets action, and a Slack action. On Make, it is a scenario with the same modules on a canvas. On n8n, it is a workflow with the same nodes, plus an AI agent if you want it to draft the reply as well. The workflow is the same. The difference is the price, the control, and how comfortable you are building it.
So, which one should you choose?
If you do not write code and you want something working today, choose Zapier. Start on the free plan, test one workflow, and only pay when you need more tasks.

If you want the best value, and you are building several workflows that run every day, choose Make. Its Core plan is hard to beat on price, and the visual canvas will save you time when things get complex.

If you are technical, you care about data control, or you want to build AI agents, choose n8n. Start with the hosted Starter plan, or self-host the Community Edition if you are comfortable running your own server.
There is no single winner for everyone. There is a winner for your situation. All three have a free way to start, so try the one that fits, build one real workflow, and see how it feels.

If this helped you decide, subscribe to Whizz AI, because next week I will show you how to build that email workflow step by step, in n8n, with no code. Tell me in the comments, which tool are you using right now, Zapier, Make, or n8n, and why? I read every comment. Thank you for watching, and I will see you in the next video.

Today, we delve into the secrets of running a profitable design service with none other than Brett Williams, the mastermind behind DesignJoy.
Subscribe for more web design videos and tutorials: https://bit.ly/3IUiVpj
🚀Ready to Scale Your Design Business Without Extra Overhead? Get access to my free course here: https://bradhussey.hopp.to/wix-studio-course

As a solo design entrepreneur, Brett has transformed his one-man design agency into a thriving business, and he's here to share his invaluable insights and tips on how to achieve freelancer success and design agency growth. By watching today’s video you’ll discover the power of pricing strategies for design agencies as Brett unravels the key components to pricing design services effectively. You’ll also learn how to run a design business like a pro as Brett shares his practical design agency tips. From managing client relationships to streamlining design workflows and delivering exceptional results.

Get started with designing your next website with Wix Studio (previously known as Editor X):
https://bradhussey.hopp.to/wixstudio

Connect with me on:
Website: https://bit.ly/3DugDfI
Instagram: https://bit.ly/3uKtjuV
Facebook: https://bit.ly/3DtW5nD
Twitter: https://bit.ly/3K2gBy4
TikTok: https://bit.ly/3Dz3C4E

New to the channel? My name’s Brad Hussey. I'm a web designer and I’ve partnered with Editor X to create an inspiring, educational, and world-class YouTube channel and community for professional web designers and design agencies who are mastering the art, business, and craft of web design. On this channel, I’ll show you how to build websites with little code. I’ll also cover topics like, choosing fonts for web design, layout design for websites, and tons of Editor X tips and tricks videos and guides to get you started on your website creation process.

Learn how to make responsive websites and join us every week for new web designer tutorials, Editor X videos, livestreams, and challenges.

metadata.title: Secret to Running a $1 Million Solo Design Agency
metadata.author: The Futur
metadata.shortDescription:
In the video, Chris and Brett discuss the advantages of subscription-based pricing for design services. Brett explains that his agency, Design Joy, is a one-man design subscription service that he started in 2017, following a layoff from a traditional design agency. He saw an opportunity in the market for a subscription-based service for higher-end design work and decided to start his own agency. He targets clients who want ongoing design work, such as branding, product design, and landing page design.

Brett compares the subscription model to a retainer, but explains that it is more productized, with fixed outcomes and a fixed fee. He likens the pricing page of a software product to the way he sells design services. His clients pay a recurring fee of $5,000 per month for unlimited requests, unlimited revisions, and a two-to-three day turnaround on requests. The outcome is fixed, but the actual volume of output can vary depending on the client's needs.

Brett discusses the advantages of subscription-based pricing over hourly or project-based pricing. He notes that it provides stability for both the client and the designer, as clients know what they are paying for and designers know what they are delivering. He also talks about the importance of trust and communication with clients, and how subscription-based pricing can help build that trust.

The conversation ends with a discussion of the potential for high revenue through subscription-based pricing, and the importance of sharing transparently to help others in the industry. Bret shares his experience of earning $120,000 per month from 20 clients, but emphasizes that this is not a model that everyone should follow blindly. He encourages designers to find their own path and share their experiences with others.

metadata.title: Brett Williams of Designjoy Answers Tough Questions About His Million-Dollar Design Job | 13
metadata.author: The Creative Brief Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Brett reveals how he transformed his solo design agency into a groundbreaking, productized service, generating an eye-popping $120K monthly revenue - that's nearly $1.5M a year as a solopreneur! But is Designjoy's success too miraculous to be true?

Welcome to the Creative Brief, a hangout with your favorite creatives, entrepreneurs, and influencers. 

Today, I’m sitting down with Brett Williams, the godfather of design subscriptions, to talk about the massive success of his company Designjoy. Brett has figured out a way to turn his one-man design agency into a productized service that grosses over $120K in monthly revenue. If you’re doing the math, that sets him up to do nearly $1.5M per year as a solopreneur. 

Now, even though I’m a fan of Brett, I went into this interview with a healthy level of skepticism. I mean, Designjoy seems too good to be true right? And it’s fair to say people have pretty strong opinions about Designjoy and Brett’s approach to viral marketing. I’m curious to know what you think after hearing him out, so let me know in the comments. 

0:00: Introduction
2:40: Brett’s Background
4:44: The Designjoy Origin Story 
9:16: Launching Designjoy and Gaining Initial Traction
13:08: Pricing and How the Subscription Model Works
16:07: Volume and the Reality of the Business
17:54: “Racing to the Bottom” Criticisms and Misconceptions
20:02: Talking About Money and Course Boys
21:27: Challenging the Conventional Design Process
23:20: Assumption-Based Design
26:22: The 30-Minute Rebrand
27:14: Challenges and Downsides of Scaling
29:29: Value-Based Pricing and the Designjoy client profile
31:59: Launching the Productize Yourself Course
35:59: Approach to Social Media
39:13: Fake Stripe Accusations and Criticisms in the Comment Section
42:23: The Vertical Integration of the Service, the Course, and the New Product
43:15: Building Aktive, a Designjoy-Inspired Project Management Tool
46:48: Brett’s Take on the Design Industry and the Rise of the Productized Model
51:51: The Problem Aktive Will Solve
53:07: Tips for Productizing Yourself: Specializing and Time to Value
57:42: Turnover and Client Churn
59:08: Closing Remarks and Rethinking the Cybertruck Order
1:02:57: Post Game Analysis

More from Brett Williams:

metadata.author: Demandflow
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video I share how we've built a sustainable productised service at DemandFlow over the last 5+ years.

LINKS
Website: https://www.demandflow.co/
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thestephenwise_/
Twitter: https://twitter.com/stephen_wise_

RESOURCES + TOOLS WE USE
Webflow: https://webflow.grsm.io/stephenwise

segments.text: if you're even remotely interested in
the web design freelancer and agency
world then you've probably seen hundreds
if not thousands of screenshots that
look like this and alongside them you'll
probably have someone telling you about
how great running a productize service
is and as someone who's run some form of
productize service for over four years
now they are pretty great but they're
not perfect and with everyone now
preaching about running a product TI
service this really raises three
questions first why do they work second
why do the absolute largest agencies not
offer them and third how do you make
salt and pepper chicken from scratch I
mean third how do you actually build a
sustainable productize service so let's
start at the beginning why do they
actually work in the first place well a
producti service is really valuable
because it simplifies the service
industry so instead of this weird
flirting period of time you have with a
client where you're trying to sus out if
the client wants to work with you
they're going to figure out what your
rate is they're going to try to
understand what it is that you do and
while you're going through this whole
process you're also trying to do the
same for them you're trying to figure
out how much money can they afford
you're trying to figure out if you
actually want to work with them and how
much you're going to quote in your
proposal now what a productize service
does is it really lets you skip the
foreplay and get straight into doing the
work and for the right client this is
great because they can just get straight
to work a lot of them don't want to have
to spend a bunch of time scoping out a
project sometimes they don't even know
what the actual full scope of the
project is so in an environment like a
startup this type of culture is
absolutely huge it also helps the
company that they know exactly how much
they'll be paying you every single month
there's no unexpected invoices there's
no large scope projects they know that
they're going to pay you this amount
every single month and they expect you
to do the work it also means that they
are not locked into long-term contracts
which is something that a lot of large
agencies do and the other reason it
could be really appealing to certain
companies is that they can hire top rate
talent and it doesn't take them very
long to hire them and it's also cheaper
than hiring someone in house and for the
person actually providing the service is
great because you can build consistent
monthly recurring income you don't have
to do custom quotes you don't have to
spend loads of time scoping out projects
and negotiating on prices and going back
and forth and changing those tiny little
line items in your deliverables but the
other thing here is that it's actually
easier to Market this now if you think
about a productize service you think
about marketing one specific thing
because you're packaging everything up
and selling one product whereas if
you're selling a typical service the
chances are that it's completely
undefined you could offer so many custom
solutions that what you have to do is
you have to Market kind of a bit of
everything you have to kind of say yeah
I I do that I can do this I can do a bit
of everything but if you are just
marketing producti service it becomes a
lot easier because you're just pushing
the same thing over and over again and
then when you actually work with the
client that's when you're kind of
defining the work that you're doing with
them now there are plenty of drawbacks
on both sides and I'll touch on these a
little bit later when I tell you exactly
how I run a product type service
business but first let's explore why the
absolute largest agencies do not provide
productized services now as much as the
midwit want to cry about how services
like design Joy are scamming or they're
faking numbers they are in fact real and
they're achievable but there's a reason
that large agencies don't follow this
model and that reason is that they can
actually charge way more money by
providing custom offers to their clients
now if you think about it if you're
selling a producti service you could
sell that to a tiny startup or you could
sell it to Amazon you'd be charging them
exactly the same price maybe you had a
few different tiers so maybe it would be
incrementally a little bit more but the
chances are you wouldn't be charging a
Nerf if you think about offering a
service to someone like Amazon why would
you charge them the exact same amount
you would charge to a tiny startup and
why would you try to sell them the same
solution as everyone else you could
easily charge someone like Amazon five
times what you could charge anyone else
and when you add in the unknown capacity
of a productize service when people say
that you can add unlimited requests but
they're going to work on one request at
a time it's like how you meant to know
how many requests are going to actually
be completed how long things are going
to take like what the actual output is
large companies do not want this people
making the decisions in these large
companies they want a tailored custom
solution and they're happy to pay more
money for that custom solution because
they can then make the decision and know
that making this decision to work with
this custom offer agency is not going to
get them fired now of course a product I
service can actually scale really nicely
into a few million P but it's very hard
to reach past this point so you can see
why the absolute largest agencies don't
follow this model now for most of us the
reality is that we're not working with
clients like Amazon we might be working
with smaller companies with startups
with growing companies so what's great
about producti service is that it can
still scale to Millions per year and a
lot of us are not looking to go past
this point because running a large
agency isn't something that appeals to
us but when you look in the larger
landscape of agencies you can see why
they don't follow the producti service
model because why would they build the
same to absolutely everyone now a lot of
them will have subscriptions set up so
they will have a striped subscription
that looks like a productize service but
they're not marketing it to everyone but
if you're not looking to build an
absolutely huge agency and you just want
to know how to build build a sustainable
producti service then I'm just going to
walk you through exactly what I've
learned in the last four and a bit 5
years and cover everything that we do to
charge High ticket retainers to clients
and those clients are happy to pay for
it so first of all let's jump into some
context most producti Services fall into
the Trap of product tize Services
because what happens when you run a
product tize service in the traditional
model is that you end up constantly
context switching you spend half your
time figuring out exactly what it is
that you should be doing because if you
think that you have a load of different
clients and all these different clients
want you to do a specific task at that
time what ends up happening is you spend
half your time just figuring out what
the most important thing to do that day
is and then what it is you should be
focused on and if you know anything
about productivity you know that this is
a really bad way to operate and what
this typical model does is it rewards
getting the low impact High urgency
tasks done so there is no planning ahead
and everything is just I need to do this
thing ASAP and it's a really small
update that we don't think about in the
larger scheme of Designing and building
a website but one of the worst things
about running a company like this is
it's almost impossible for you to plan
your workload because if you think on a
Monday you have no idea what you're
going to be doing on a Thursday so it's
very difficult to plan your week out in
advance it's also really really
difficult to actually take any form of
holiday unless you have other people
doing the work for you and honestly one
of the worst parts of this and this is
something that I offered for quite a
while is that clients just don't know
what to expect they don't know when the
work is actually going to come in they
don't have any sort of consistency in
terms of when it is that you'll
communicate with them there is just
nothing that they can expect from your
workload so instead we taken a different
approach to the productize service and
essentially turned it into a retainer
productized service and with this what
we do is we work with startups and
marketing teams so most of the time
these companies are growing most of the
time they will have a large marketing
team let's say at least five people and
with them what we do is we consistently
make updates run campaigns do testing
optimize for conversion rate and most of
the time these types of companies really
value brand so they value good design
they value actually doing things
properly now the reason that these teams
will Outsource to US versus doing it
inous is that they have this internal
struggle where they typically have a
product design team they'll have a
product development team and then
they'll have a marketing team now the
biggest problem that the marketing team
have is that every time they want to
make an update to the website they'll
have to ask the product team but the
product team is so busy building the
product that there is no one to actually
make these changes for them and often
the marketing team's not big enough to
Warrant someone to work on this
full-time so instead they're kind of in
this limbo where they're either waiting
for someone else to do the change or
they have to go in and try and make
these changes themselves so what we
essentially become is an extension on
their marketing team and this solves a
lot of problems for them because as soon
as a marketing team want to run a new
campaign as soon as they want to do
something they know they have the
capacity to do that so essentially what
it is that we run is a productized
retainer and a productized retainer is a
really good model to build your business
from because what you're doing is you're
figuring out what the workload actually
is with that client whether that's one
day a week two days a week whatever that
amount of work that they need is you're
then delivering that amount of work to
them and you're working with them
consistently over a long period of time
now let's just jump into exactly how our
internal system works so in terms of
onboarding what we'll do is we'll
typically have a sales
then when the company signs up they'll
get an email confirmation which is
something we just recently set up then
internally we need to set things up we
need to figure out what day of the week
it is that we're going to be working
with that client or if it's multiple
days a week then we have our internal
team assigned to this so the way that we
work is we have a designer a developer
and then a role called a project lead a
Project Lead is someone who can do both
design and development they can do the
quality assurance and they can also
communicate and kind of manage the
project with the client essentially what
we have is a team of three people
working on any one client's account then
what's going to happen is we'll get
everything set up and the Project Lead
is going to intro the client explain the
system that we use and invite everyone
to all the different accounts so what we
have is clickup for task management we
then have a shared Google Drive we then
have a shared slack inside of that slack
everything is pinned so people know
exactly where these different resources
are whenever they need them and then
once we' got everything on boarded and
everyone knows exactly what it is that
they're doing
it's time to get to work now the way
that the work actually happens is we
just have a super simple system inside a
clickup inside of here we have a backlog
this week current request awaiting
feedback and complete now the client
adds tasks to the backlog now they can
do this either through the form or they
can do it manually inside a clickup
themselves then the Project Lead will go
back and forth with the client inside a
slack and just determine what it is that
they want to get done this week what the
highest priority things are inside of
the task management system we also have
priority and we have size of task inside
of there as custom statuses that way we
can see the overall workload and the
backlog is really a place for us to
start planning what it is that we're
going to execute on over the next few
weeks and next few months so once the
client has added the task into the
backlog maybe they've assigned a
priority a due date if it is needed and
maybe they've estimated the size of the
task but they don't always have to do
this the Project Lead will then pick up
the task they will move it into this
week based on what it is that we're
going to be working on for this week
they'll go back and forth with the
client just to make sure they have the
priorities straight and they know
exactly what it is that we want to be
doing then what we're going to do on the
active work day is we're going to go and
work through each of those tasks one by
one so with a typical product TI service
the biggest thing that they do and
probably the worst thing they do for a
client but the best thing they do for
themselves is that they only work on one
task at a time and then they will move
that task across to like for review from
the client and then they won't work on
anything else so what happens is you
have this really slow process where
maybe they'll do a little bit of work
send it for review and then the person
will have to come back and then they'll
do that again and that how people run
these produ high service businesses and
sure it does work and a lot of clients
do still find that valuable But
ultimately what happens is you just
don't complete that much work because
all they're doing is a little bit of
work and then sending it over so instead
what we do is we try to have a kind of
full day of work and what we'll do is
we'll work through every single one in
terms of priority once we worked on a
specific task let's say it's a designer
designing something they'll then send it
over to the Project Lead the Project
Lead will do any form of QA so quality
assurance if there's any revisions we'll
just go back and forth with the designer
on those revisions the project leads
then going to go and update that task
inside a clickup they're then going to
message the client inside of slack and
just say hey like here is the update now
often what we'll do is we'll work
through all the different updates for
that day and then send one condensed
slack message with all all the different
things that they need to do after that
if any revisions are needed we'll then
just make sure we're doing that inside
of markup is if it's for the website and
figma if it's a design change and then
that cycle just repeats again for the
next week the Project Lead is just going
to assign which tasks is going to be
done that week and then we're going to
communicate with the client on the
priority and we're going to go through
this whole process again and again now
that is literally everything we do in
terms of our internal product High
service retainer as I mentioned I've
been running some variation of this for
over 4 years now from freelancer to
running a studio and for me this is by
far the best iteration of this whole
productized service model sure it
doesn't seem quite as appealing as the
idea of giving them unlimited requests
and working on one at a time and working
for them at all times but then also not
working for them at all times but
ultimately this just means that the
client is happy and we're happy and we
know exactly the amount of work that
we're going to be doing each week as I
mentioned the ability to actually batch
your work is way more valuable than just
a scattered approach where you just do
these tiny little tasks here and there
and never spend a huge amount of time on
one specific thing if you have
experienced running a product I service
I'd love to know exactly how you operate
your service because this kind of thing
is absolutely fascinating to me and
there are so many different variations
as to how you can do this but these
smallest little tweaks make all the
difference in terms of if you're happy
internally working on that thing and you
can do that for a long period of time
and also what the client's expecting and
what the client is getting and
ultimately if they're actually happy
with your service as always thank you
very much for watching watching and I'll
catch you in the next one

metadata.title: This Designer Makes $2M a Year With ZERO Employees (Designjoy Explained Simply)
metadata.author: I Make it Simple
metadata.shortDescription:
One designer. No employees. No meetings. And by his own account, about $2M a year. How does Designjoy, a design business run entirely by founder Brett Williams, actually work? In this episode of I Make it Simple we break it down for beginners, using only what the official site and Brett himself have said publicly.

What you'll learn:
- What a "productized service" is, in plain English
- The weekend launch and the $80K-a-month side project
- How a flat $4,995/month design subscription works
- Why a flat price makes money even when clients use it less
- How the price went from $450 to $4,995
- 3 lessons you can use if you're just starting out

Chapters
0:00 One designer, $2M a year
0:11 What Designjoy is
0:21 The weekend launch
0:28 $80K a month... and a day job
0:35 60+ job applications
0:42 Not hours: a subscription
0:45 The $4,995 plan
0:51 How the request board works
1:01 Where the idea came from
1:16 The clever bit: a flat price
1:30 From $450 to $4,995
1:40 20-25 clients, ~6 hours a day
1:52 3 lessons for beginners
2:07 Good + fast: the honest warning
2:16 Your turn

Sources (figures as stated by each source)
- Designjoy official site (launched 2017, run entirely by Brett, no extra designers or outsourcing, $4,995/month plan, one request at a time, ~2 business days average, pause or cancel anytime): https://www.designjoy.co/
- Brett Williams on The Growth Podcast with Aakash Gupta, Jun 2025 ("$2M/year one-person business", built over a weekend, ~$80K/month while still employed, 60+ job applications after a layoff): https://www.news.aakashg.com/p/brett-designjoy-podcast
- Brett Williams with Chris Do, The Futur (Design Pickle comparison, started at $450/month, 20-25 clients, ~6 hours a day, 20-25% of clients underuse the service): https://thefutur.com/watch/how-to-run-a-million-dollar-solo-design-agency
- "20 x $5,000 = ~$100,000/month" is our own simple math, not a reported figure. The request board shown is an illustration.

This channel is independent and not sponsored by or affiliated with Designjoy. This is one rare result, not typical income and not a promise of earnings.

What skill could YOU turn into a subscription? Tell me in the comments.

#designjoy #productizedservice #onepersonbusiness

metadata.title: We Tested Bland AI’s Voice Agent. Here’s What Happened
metadata.author: CX Foundation
metadata.shortDescription:
In this live demo, Catherine from the CX Foundation tests Bland AI’s voice agent to see how it performs in real customer service scenarios.

Bland AI is a voice AI and conversational AI platform built for enterprise teams, with features like proprietary infrastructure, dedicated customer instances, and conversational pathways designed to help reduce hallucinations and guide AI phone agents through structured workflows.

In this demo, we put Bland AI’s voice agent through practical CX tests, including lead qualification, interruption handling, topic switching, guardrails, language handling, ambiguity resolution, silence handling, objection handling, escalation triggers, and tool execution.

We also evaluate where the agent performed well, including natural conversation flow, pricing discussion, silence handling, and audio adaptation, while also looking at key limitations such as live agent transfer, SMS follow-up, and email follow-up.

If you are exploring voice AI agents, AI phone agents, contact center automation, customer service AI, or enterprise conversational AI platforms, this demo gives you a practical look at what Bland AI can currently do in a live customer interaction.

#BlandAI #VoiceAI #AIAgents

01:27 Test 2 — Lead Qualification
01:58 Test 3 — Interruption & Information Capture
02:44 Test 4 — Topic Switching
03:12 Test 5 — Guardrail Testing
03:25 Test 6 — AI Disclosure & Audio Adaptation
03:47 Test 7 — Language Handling
04:02 Test 8 — Ambiguity Resolution
04:20 Test 9 — Silence Handling
04:40 Test 10 — Objection Handling
05:04 Test 11 — Escalation Trigger
05:32 Test 12 — Tool Execution
05:57 Test 13 — Call Closing
06:22 Demo Performance Review
07:50 Catherine Closing Remarks

Over the last two months, I've tested every major voice AI tool. In this video I compare Vapi and Bland AI head-to-head in 7 areas – from build experience and voice realism, to latency (my own data) and costs. If you have any questions about either platform drop them in the comments below and I'll do my best to answer.

If it's your first view — hey 👋 I'm Marcus! I spent 12 years building an 7-figure software venture studio (we built 12 businesses – 6 failed, 4 held, 2 exited). https://www.youtube.com/@intellagents?sub_confirmation=1

Some of these are affiliate links, which means I'll receive a small commission if you use them without any additional cost for you. This helps support the channel and allows me to continue making videos like this. Thank you for the support 🙏

metadata.title: Retell AI vs Bland AI (Don't choose WRONG!)
metadata.author: Voice AI Decoded
metadata.shortDescription:
⚖️ Compare them: https://voiceai.guide/bland-vs-retell/
➡️ Retell AI: https://dashboard.retellai.com/?ref=voiceaiguide-yt
➡️ Bland: https://bland.ai

Over the last two months, I've tested every major voice AI tool. In this video I compare Retell AI and Bland AI head-to-head in 7 areas – from build experience and voice realism, to latency (my own data) and costs. If you have any questions about either platform drop them in the comments below and I'll do my best to answer. 

*Why watch?*
If it's your first view — hey 👋 I'm Marcus! I spent 12 years building an 7-figure software venture studio (we built 12 businesses – 6 failed, 4 held, 2 exited). I've always loved building automated businesses and sharing my weird and wonderful workflows. You can check out my main channel on AI automation here ⤵️
https://www.youtube.com/@intellagents?sub_confirmation=1

Some of these are affiliate links, which means I'll receive a small commission if you use them without any additional cost for you. This helps support the channel and allows me to continue making videos like this. Thank you for the support 🙏

And all you need to do is enter the MCP server URL and then any headers or query parameters that you need to authenticate it. But I do point it out because it is a relative weakness of retail. Most voice AI tools I use have a much broader range of native integrations, but retail does not. So that brings me on to another point which is concurrency. So, this is an important concept when building voice agents because particularly if you're doing outbound calls or if you have busy periods and quiet periods, if you have 10 customers all calling you at once, you don't want to only have one phone line. That means everyone's kind of on hold for ages. So, by default, you can have up to 20 concurrent calls on retail, which is pretty generous. And they've also got this handy feature called concurrency burst, where if you get a sudden influx of calls, instead of putting everyone on hold or forcing you to buy extra phone lines, you just pay a slightly higher rate. And this works for up to three times your normal limit. So essentially 60 concurrent calls. If you consistently have a higher number of concurrent calls, you're running a call center for example, you can of course adjust your limit and it cost $8 per additional concurrent phone line, which again is pretty reasonable. So let's talk about latency. So the first thing I really like about retail is they make this transparent. This is not true of all voice AI platforms. So when you're building your voice agent, you can see up here in the top bar the estimated latency for your agent. And this is quite handy because it gives you an indication if you suddenly add a really massive global prompt that's going to push up the latency. You can also see things for example like changing the model either using the fast tier or something like GPT 4.1 nano. You should see an instant reduction in the latency and generally from my experience with retail it is slightly on the pessimistic side. So generally I find that my actual latency is often slightly better than this. So coming on to that point, if you go into your call logs, you can see your actual latency. And another thing I really like about this is you can see the breakdown. So you don't just get this kind of one number. So here you can see 756 milliseconds, which is roughly what I see on average. So when I've done standardized latency testing across different tools, I believe with retail I was getting 714 milliseconds of endtoend latency. That is not the best I've seen, but it is still very good. It's still in the realms of sounding natural and being very usable for a production voice agent. Thing I really like is that if you hover over here, you can get the breakdown of where that latency is happening. So you can see is it at the speechto text stage, is it the LLM or is it at the texttospech voice engine. And this is really helpful because it tells you where the problem is and therefore what you can do to improve and optimize it. This is quite rare to see in voice agent platforms. There's only one or two other platforms I can think of that actually give you this information. And for me, this just tells me like retail is not trying to hide anything. They're giving you this information so you can do something with it and actually make your voice agent better. So in this case, for example, it's clear that we do not have a latency problem at the transcription stage, but we might want to tighten up our prompts or use a different model for the LLM inference and possibly we might want to have a play around with the the voice engine, but big wins are going to be at the LLM stage. So just really helpful. Now let's touch on costs. Now, generally speaking, when you add everything up, so like the LLM cost, telefan costs, etc., retail comes out around about 13 cents per minute. Now, obviously that is going to depend on the model you choose, the telefan options, there's dozens of things that affect this number, but generally for a standard tech stack, so GP4.1 deep transcription and 11 Labs Turbo V2, this is roughly going to be about right. It is not the absolute cheapest option for voice agents, but it's generally very reasonable. Anything under about 14 15 cents per minute is pretty decent. So, for me, retail is a really solid option. It gets a lot of the boring stuff like testing, latency, concurrency, it gets all these things right, but it also just makes it really easy to build production quality voice agents. So, if you're nontechnical, if you like building in no code, and you don't want to be in the weeds building voice agents via an API, Retail for me is about as good as it gets. So, next up, let's have a look at Bland AI. So Bland is one of the most powerful platforms for building voice agents on. It does have a bit of a learning curve to it and I wouldn't recommend it to beginners, but it's pretty impressive how much stuff you can customize inside the bland platform. So easiest way to get started in bland is probably with conversational pathways. This gives you a nice kind of visual flow editor for building your agent on. So if we go into this one for example, you can see like a lot of platforms, you can build out your agents on this kind of nice canvas where each part of the conversation can be represented by a node and then you can create different conditions for what to do based on how the caller responds. We can test our agent directly in the platform. So you don't have to hook this up to a phone number or have it call your phone just to test it, which is quite nice. Also, the testing functionality inside Bland is very mature. This is something that tends to set apart the good tools from the less good tools is things like having evaluations and good QA features for testing your agents because this is something that kind of starts to become more and more important when you start shipping agents to production. In terms of telefan, if we go over to phone numbers, you can buy phone numbers directly inside the bland platform. They are $15 a month, which is relatively expensive, and they're only US numbers. So, generally speaking with Bland, you would almost certainly want to bring your own Twilio, which you can do here, or you can do it via SIP trunk, but you need to but you'd need to contact Bland to do that. Now, in most voice AI platforms, when you're building your agent, you just select the voice off of 11 Labs that you want, and you're kind of done. Bland AI go one step further, and I really like how they approach this. So, with Bland AI, you create a persona, which you then attach to your workflow or your AI voice agent. And this just gives you a lot more control. It means you don't have to put all this information in the global prompt, but it also means you can customize your agent in a bit more detail. So, you can of course set the the voice engine that you're using here. You can set things like background noise, all stuff you'd usually expect. You can also add the prompt for things like behavior, tone, turn taking, all that sort of stuff. And you can also upload knowledge here. So, this to me just makes a bit more sense doing it this way, adding this information to your persona here. And then you can kind of connect those personas to the conversational pathway. So latency wise, Bland is very good. Unfortunately, they don't give you too much information on the exact latency, but if you kind of read between the lines and look at the time stamps between different steps, generally speaking in bland, I'm getting between 450 and 650 milliseconds of latency, which is very good. Definitely puts Bland up there as one of the best tools. The best I've seen on average is Vappy, which is about 514 milliseconds. So on a good day, Bland slightly beats that. On a less good day, it's a little bit below. Obviously, it's going to change depending on things like models and the prompts you're using, but generally speaking, I've not run into any latency issues with Bland. Now, let's talk about pricing. So, I believe pricing is not public on their website, but you can see it on their platform here. Generally speaking, it all kind of averages down to around about 12 cents per minute, 11 cents per minute, which is actually pretty reasonable. It's not the most affordable I've seen. I'd say the cheapest at the moment would be around about eight cents n cents per minute, but a lot of voice agent platforms average around about 14 15 cents per minute. And in terms of limits that you get around concurrency, they're all pretty reasonable as well. So for $300 a month, you've got 50 concurrent call lines, which is pretty generous and that can be bumped up to virtually unlimited if you go up onto the enterprise plan. So both of these are great options for building voice agents on. And given that you can try both of them out for free, I'd recommend doing that to see which one's going to be a better fit for your use case. Now, I'll drop links to both of them below, as well as the side-by-side comparison that I put together. And if you'd like to watch me live build the same voice agent on both platforms, as well as four other voice AI tools, and then live test them with real phone calls, you can check that video out

metadata.shortDescription:
https://vapi.ai/?aff=intellagents-ZVSDm5siKr4 (*VAPI $10 FREE)

In this VAPI tutorial, I'll walk you through creating an AI receptionist from scratch in just 15 minutes. You'll learn the basics of setting up your first AI agent, including initial conversation flows and integrating with essential tools like Google Calendar to manage bookings and appointments automatically.

Beyond the initial setup, we'll delve into optimising your voice agent for real-world scenarios. Discover how to handle edge cases gracefully, such as transferring calls to a human agent or suggesting alternative times when a slot is unavailable. We'll also cover crucial aspects like crafting effective global prompts, using variables for better data capture, and selecting the right AI models (like GPT-4.1) to balance cost, quality, and latency. By the end, you'll understand why VAPI stands out among other voice AI tools for its affordability and impressive performance, making it one of the easiest ways to build voice AI.

metadata.title: ElevenLabs vs Vapi vs Retell AI: I Built the Same AI Receptionist on All 3
metadata.author: Stephanie Nyarko
metadata.shortDescription:
I Built on All Three Voice Agent Platforms ... Here's What I Found (Retell, Vapi, ElevenLabs)

AI voice agents can save you hours and help you serve more clients—but which platform should you actually build on: ElevenLabs, Vapi, or Retell AI?

I built the same AI receptionist on all three platforms and compared them on the things that actually matter when you’re building voice AI for a business: cost, setup time, flexibility, and call quality. In this video, you’ll see where ElevenLabs, Vapi, and Retell AI each shine—and the trade-offs you should know before committing to one.

If you’re a solopreneur building your first AI receptionist, ElevenLabs offers a fast setup and excellent voice quality out of the box. If you’re an agency that needs more control over LLMs, text-to-speech providers, call routing, webhooks, CRM integrations, and client configurations, Vapi gives you much more flexibility. Retell AI sits between the two, combining an easier setup with enough customization for more advanced business use cases.

I also break down estimated costs using the same small-business receptionist scenario, compare the setup experience, and explain why the cheapest AI voice agent isn’t necessarily the best choice. Your time, your client’s requirements, and the quality of the caller experience matter much more than a small difference in monthly platform costs.

By the end, you’ll know which platform makes sense for your first client, a growing AI automation agency, or a more customized voice AI deployment.

metadata.shortDescription:
1️⃣ Get started with Bland AI 👉 https://www.bland.ai
2️⃣ Join my new AI Community for FREE! 👉 https://www.papareact.com/ztoh-form

AI voice agents are getting seriously powerful — and in this video, I show you how to build an AI receptionist that can answer calls, sound human, use a business knowledge base, book appointments, trigger tools, and update real data while the conversation is happening.

We’ll build around a dental clinic example using Bland AI, Norm, knowledge bases, pathways, Cal.com, web widgets, the Bland Web Agent SDK, Convex endpoints, MCP, and the Bland CLI. By the end, you’ll see how to ship an AI receptionist for your own business or clients without stitching together a messy voice stack from scratch.

🎯 What You'll learn:
✅ How Bland AI handles human-like phone conversations with low-latency voice agents
✅ How to create an AI receptionist persona with voices, behavior settings, and inbound call flows
✅ How to upload a knowledge base so your agent answers from real business information
✅ How Norm can build, test, and self-fix an agent workflow for you
✅ How to connect appointment booking with Cal.com tool calls
✅ How pathways route calls between questions, booking flows, and wrap-up steps
✅ How to add a Bland web widget directly to a website
✅ How to use the Bland Web Agent SDK for custom app integrations
✅ How MCP and the Bland CLI let coding agents create and debug voice agents
✅ Why self-hosting and compliance matter for healthcare, finance, legal, and enterprise use cases
+ SO MUCH MORE!

🕣 Timestamps:
00:00 Intro | Live AI phone call demo
01:07 What we’re building today
02:12 Why Bland sounds so human
03:12 Sign up and open the Bland dashboard
04:05 Create an AI receptionist persona
05:30 Inbound numbers, SMS, and behavior settings

The TRUTH About Selling AI Automations 🤯

Most marketing pushing you to start an AI automation agency promises 200K to 300K per month. The reality is much harder. My first startup got acquired by a pioneer in the robotic process automation space, and I have spent years watching workflow automation get rebranded as "AI automation" the moment a single step in the workflow calls an AI tool. Workflow automation is genuinely valuable. Building an agency to sell it to other businesses is a completely different problem.

This video expands on Zubair Trabzada's original take on the AI automation agency model. Credit goes to Zubair for the framing on agency revenue expectations and the comparison with information products. His original video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XUYvDbAv1IA

Inside this one I lay out three reasons selling AI automations to businesses is harder than the marketing implies, the realistic revenue band most agency owners actually land in, why information products and SaaS scale differently, and the exact technical and team profile that makes the AI automation agency model viable when it is the right fit.

📌 What you'll learn:
→ Why the AI automation agency model is essentially AI consulting with extra technical risk on top
→ The messy company systems problem and what nobody tells you about debugging workflow automations
→ The realistic revenue band for a small AI automation agency in 2026
→ Why scaling beyond 100K per month requires a real team, not a solo operator
→ The information product and SaaS comparison, including 3x to 20x revenue multiples on acquisition
→ When an AI automation agency actually is the right path, and who should not start one

If you have been sold on the dream of 300K per month from a solo AI automation agency, this is the reality check. Workflow automation has been around for decades. Sticking an AI API call inside it does not change how the underlying business model scales.
