metadata.title: Introducing RAG 2.0: Agentic RAG + Knowledge Graphs (FREE Template)
metadata.author: Cole Medin
metadata.shortDescription:
Traditional RAG systems only scratch the surface of what's possible. In this video, I cover an advanced AI agent I created as a free system for you that combines vector search with knowledge graphs to create a powerhouse of an agent that understands relationships, tracks knowledge changes over time, and reasons about complex connections between pieces of information.

This agent is very extendable and built with PostgreSQL + pgvector for semantic search and Neo4j + Graphiti for temporal knowledge graphs. It automatically chooses between vector search, graph traversal, or hybrid approaches based on the query.

I built the full package here - a complete implementation including semantic chunking, a vector database/knowledge graph pipeline, a FastAPI backend with streaming responses, and a CLI tool to chat with the agent.

Full source code (linked below!) included with support for multiple LLM providers. This is production-ready RAG.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Neon's free tier is more than enough to cover what you'll need in this guide! But if you do decide that you need to upgrade, you can sign up through this link and get a $100 credit:

https://get.neon.com/2cm

I partnered with Neon to get this for you!

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Code and instructions for this Agentic RAG Agent here:

https://github.com/coleam00/ottomator-agents/tree/main/agentic-rag-knowledge-graph

Local AI Package (includes Neo4j for knowledge graphs):

https://github.com/coleam00/local-ai-packaged

Graphiti (open source on GitHub):

https://github.com/getzep/graphiti

Weaviate article on Agentic RAG:

https://weaviate.io/blog/what-is-agentic-rag

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

00:00 - Introducing Agentic RAG + Knowledge Graphs
01:05 - Unleashing the Power of the Agent Live
05:21 - Tech Stack for this Agent (Pydantic AI, Graphiti, Postgres, etc.)
06:31 - What is Agentic RAG and Why is it so Useful?
10:36 - Set up this Agentic RAG Agent for Yourself!
12:53 - Database Setup in Neon
14:00 - Installing Neo4j
15:07 - Environment Configuration (LLMs, DB, Neo4j, etc.)
18:17 - Setting up Our Knowledge Base for RAG
22:35 - Defining How Your Agent Searches
24:47 - Running and Testing the AI Agent
28:11 - How I used Claude Code to Build this Agent
38:22 - Final Thoughts

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Join me as I push the limits of what is possible with AI. I'll be uploading videos every week - Wednesdays at 7:00 PM CDT!

metadata.title: Knowledge Graph or Vector Database… Which is Better?
metadata.author: Adam Lucek
metadata.shortDescription:
In the evolving landscape of AI and information retrieval, knowledge graphs have emerged as a powerful way to represent complex, interconnected information. But how do they work, and are they better than traditional RAG setups?

Resources:
Notebook Repo - https://github.com/ALucek/GraphRAG-Breakdown
GraphRAG - https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/
GraphRAG Paper - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.16130
GraphRAG Case Study from LinkedIN - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.17723
Unifying Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.08302
The Ultimate Guide to Fine-Tuning LLMs - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.13296
Google’s Knowledge Graph Introduction - https://blog.google/products/search/introducing-knowledge-graph-things-not/
Leiden Algorithm - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leiden_algorithm

Chapters:
00:00 - Why RAG Fails
01:54 - What is a Knowledge Graph?
03:35 - Knowledge Graphs & LLMs
05:39 - Introducing GraphRAG
06:17 - Main Components of Knowledge Graphs
07:39 - Setting up GraphRAG
11:10 - Data Flow: Overview
12:13 - Data Flow: Entity & Relationship Extraction
16:40 - Data Flow: Community Clustering
18:28 - Data Flow: Community Report Generation
20:11 - Observing Final Knowledge Graph
22:12 - RAG Setup
23:58 - RAG: Local Search
27:10 - RAG: Global Search
30:23 - RAG: DRIFT Search
35:06 - Comparing GraphRAG vs Regular RAG
36:59 - Comparison Discussion

metadata.title: RAG Explained: Why LLMs Hallucinate Without a Knowledge Layer
metadata.author: AI Engineering with Kaushal
metadata.shortDescription:
Your LLM is incredibly powerful.

But does it actually know your company?

Your internal policies, product documentation, architecture documents, customer FAQs, contracts, incident reports and thousands of other private documents?

Probably not.

And that's one of the biggest challenges when bringing Generative AI into the enterprise.

In this video, we break down the fundamental problem behind enterprise AI:

LLM intelligence ≠ company knowledge.

You'll learn:

What an LLM actually knows
Why an LLM doesn't automatically know your company's private information
Why simply asking an LLM company-specific questions can lead to hallucinations
The difference between intelligence and knowledge access
What Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) actually solves
How RAG connects your company knowledge with an LLM
Why RAG is becoming important for enterprise AI

This is the beginning of our RAG journey, where we'll move from the fundamentals all the way to building a real-world RAG system.

If you're interested in RAG, Enterprise AI, LLM applications, Vector Databases, Embeddings and AI Agents, subscribe and follow the complete series.

#RAG #GenerativeAI #LLM #EnterpriseAI #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #RetrievalAugmentedGeneration #LLMApplications
#RAGTutorial #RAGPipeline #EnterpriseAI #AIEngineering #LLMEngineering #GenAI #VectorDatabase #Embeddings #AIArchitecture #MachineLearning

metadata.author: KodeKloud
metadata.shortDescription:
🧪Try RAG Hands-On Labs for Free - https://kode.wiki/4oANO8s

Learn how RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) solves the challenge of connecting AI assistants like ChatGPT to massive document repositories! 

In this comprehensive video, we'll show you exactly how to make AI search, read, and understand large company documents using vector embeddings and semantic search.

Ready to build your own RAG system? Access our FREE interactive labs where you can experiment with real RAG implementations, test different chunking strategies, and see vector databases in action!

🧪Try RAG Hands-On Labs for Free - https://kode.wiki/4oANO8s

📚 What You'll Learn:
• What is RAG and why it's revolutionary for AI document search
• How vector embeddings transform documents into searchable data
• The 3-step RAG process: Retrieval, Augmented, Generation
• Semantic search vs traditional search methods
• Critical chunking strategies for different document types
• RAG Demo

🚀Explore Our Top Courses & Special Offers: https://kode.wiki/3CzuOnc

00:00 - Introduction to RAG
00:24 - Why Traditional Search Methods Don't Work
00:55 - The RAG Method Explained
01:54 - Step 1: Retrieval Process
02:25 - Step 2: Augmentation Explained
03:15 - Step 3: Generation Process
03:54 - Strategies for RAG Calibration
05:01 - Practical Lab Demo Introduction

08:16 - Demo - Launch a Simple Web Interface
09:43 - Conclusion & Free Lab Access

metadata.title: Practical GraphRAG: Making LLMs smarter with Knowledge Graphs — Michael, Jesus, and Stephen, Neo4j
metadata.author: AI Engineer
metadata.shortDescription:
RAG has become one standard architecture component for GenAI applications to address hallucinations and integrate factual knowledge. While vector search over text is common, knowledge graphs represent a proven advancement by leveraging advanced RAG patterns to access and integrate interconnected factual information, complementing the language skills of LLMs. This talk explores GraphRAG challenges, implementation patterns, and real-world agentic examples with Google's ADK, demonstrating how this approach delivers more trustworthy and explainable GenAI solutions with enhanced reasoning capabilities.

About Michael Hunger
Michael Hunger has been passionate about software development for more than 30 years.

For the last 15 years, he has been working on the open source Neo4j graph database filling many roles, most recently heading product innovation and GenAI.

As a developer Michael enjoys many aspects of software development and architecture, learning new things every day, participating in exciting and ambitious open source projects and contributing and writing software related books and articles. Michael spoke at numerous conferences and helped organize others.

Michael helps kids to learn to program by running weekly girls-only coding classes at local schools.

About Jesús Barrasa
Dr. Jesús Barrasa is the AI Field CTO at Neo4j, where he works with organisations combining the power of GenAI with Knowledge Graphs. He co-authored "Building Knowledge Graphs" (O'Reilly 2023) and is cohost of the monthly Going Meta live webcast (https://goingmeta.live/) since 2022.
Jesús holds a Ph.D. in Artificial Intelligence/Knowledge Representation and is an active thought leader in the KG and AI space.

About Stephen Chin
Stephen Chin is VP of Developer Relations at Neo4j, conference chair of the LF AI & Data Foundation, and author of numerous titles including the upcoming GraphRAG: The Definitive Guide for O'Reilly. He has given keynotes and main stage talks at numerous conferences around the world including AI Engineer Summit, AI DevSummit, Devoxx, DevNexus, JNation, JavaOne, Shift, Joker, swampUP, and GIDS. Stephen is an avid motorcyclist who has done evangelism tours in Europe, Japan, and Brazil, interviewing developers in their natural habitat. When he is not traveling, he enjoys teaching kids how to do AI, embedded, and robot programming together with his daughters.

Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. Stay up to date on our upcoming events and content by joining our newsletter here: https://www.ai.engineer/newsletter

---

Watch along with the corrected transcript, summary, timestamps and resources on this talk's official AIE page:
https://ai.engineer/talks/XNneh6-eyPg-practical-graphrag-making-llms-smarter-with-knowledge-graphs

metadata.title: Beyond the Case | Episode 6: RAG, AI Agents & Vector Databases — Without the Hype
metadata.author: Mirketa Inc
metadata.shortDescription:
RAG. AI agents. Vector databases. Embeddings. Semantic search.

These terms are everywhere in enterprise AI right now — but what do they actually mean, and how do they work together in a real customer service environment?

In Episode 6 of Beyond the Case, Clint, Rajeev, and Alec break down the practical architecture behind modern enterprise AI without the buzzwords.

We discuss:

What Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) actually does

Why an LLM alone is not enough for enterprise customer service

The difference between keyword search and semantic search

What embeddings are and why they matter

What a vector database actually does

Why chunking and metadata can make or break retrieval

How AI agents differ from chatbots

Why agents need tools, APIs, workflows, and permissions

How RAG and AI agents work together

When Salesforce, Service Cloud, Agentforce, or external AI infrastructure should be used

Why not every AI application needs a vector database

How to evaluate RAG quality and reduce hallucinations

Why “agentic” does not automatically mean autonomous

How these technologies fit into Case Rezolver and AI-powered case resolution

One of the simplest ways to think about it:

RAG helps the AI know things.
Tools help the AI do things.
Agents connect the two.

The real opportunity is not adding more AI terminology to your architecture.

It is using the right combination of retrieval, reasoning, and action to resolve customer cases faster and more consistently.

If you work in Enterprise AI, Customer Service, Technical Support, Salesforce Service Cloud, ServiceNow, Agentforce, Knowledge Management, RAG, AI Agents, or Case Management, this episode is for you.

#AI #EnterpriseAI #RAG #AIAgents #VectorDatabase #GenerativeAI #Salesforce #ServiceCloud #Agentforce #ServiceNow #CustomerService #CustomerSupport #CaseManagement #KnowledgeManagement #SemanticSearch #CaseResolution

Check out more: https://www.mirketa.com/

After retrieval, it's just as easy as when it was put in, it's readable text. >> And this becomes very useful with enterprise support data because that data inherently is messy. Historical cases are not consistently put in. Different agents use different terminology to define or document their resolutions. Semantic search lets you exact extract your information from that imperfect documentation or a history that you have. >> So, where does the vector database actually come in? >> So, a vector database is designed to store and search those embeddings efficiently. So, you take all of your knowledge content, you break it into usable pieces through chunking, and then you create embeddings for those pieces, and then you store them in a vector database. Then, when a user asks a question, you create an embedding for that question and search for similar vectors. So, basically, you're breaking the question into a bunch of numbers, and we're like, "Hey, are there any numbers here that that look like this?" And the the database will return the most relevant content, going back to my analogy, from around the room. And one thing people don't expect is that it always returns something. Ask about a problem you've never documented, and it will hand back the closest match, even when the closest match isn't really close. So, that's why a well-built system sets a minimum similarity bar instead of trusting whatever comes back first. And that's what we put a lot of work into with Case Resolver is building thresholds and confidence matching and re-ranking services that will actually take a look at the returned results and say, "This one was like the closest match we could find, but it's completely irrelevant. So, we can't give that as a good piece of evidence or an answer, but there's something down here that might have been put lower on the ranking that actually is relevant. So, let's perform a re-ranking run and move that up to the top." So, a well-built framework around it corrects for these flaws with rag. >> So, the vector database itself is not AI. >> No, it's not. That's right. And that's a common misunderstanding. The vector database doesn't do any reasoning at all. It doesn't decide what to do. It doesn't answer the customer. Its job is just retrieval. That's it. It's all mathematical. >> Yeah, and I think of this as a sophisticated way of helping AI find the right pieces of knowledge quickly. >> And so, you mentioned breaking documents into pieces. Why would you give the model the whole document at once? >> So, the reason why we wouldn't want to do that, I would say, is it large documents end up creating a lot of noise. So, imagine like a 100-page product manual that an engineer needs on the job. A customer might ask one very specific configuration issue. And if you send the entire manual to the model, you're burying the answer that they're looking for in content that's mostly irrelevant. And instead, you break it into smaller chunks. So, you get the exact section that you're looking for with the answer you need. And that helps a lot with models cuz if you're going for a system that is quick, low latency, and accurate, you're going to use a smaller model more often than not with these systems. And like I said before, it's all about the framework you build around it. So, the more context you're adding in there, the higher chance you're going to have that the model forgets its instructions or hallucinates. So, smaller chunks are better. Just the chunk that contains the answer. A section, a paragraph, a procedure. then retrieval only selects the parts that appear relevant. So, if your chunks are too large, you get unnecessary information, and if they're too small, you lose important context like getting one puzzle piece without the picture on the box. Good chunking also allows for like it follows the old document's structure, and if you split a procedure in the middle step of four, that's how you get an answer that's missing step five. So, a chunking strategy affects retrieval quality really significantly. >> And this is one of those implementation details that get skipped in the height. People think rag means connected at a to your rag database. There's so much more to making it work well. >> So, let's walk through a support example from let's say beginning to end. >> Okay. Let's we have done in earlier episodes, maybe in different context, and let's walk through again. I'll take Elixir claims related cases that we get. So, let's say a case comes in. Customer says, "Claims are suddenly being rejected after a configuration change." The system person needs to understand what the issue appears to be. Then retrieval might look for similar cases that we have had, knowledge article that we may have, release notes that we may have, customer specific configuration if we have that on file, known pair specific rules or issues that they have informed us during the day or during the week that may have come back from different pairs. >> And the retrieval layer, like it may return five highly relevant pieces of information. So, the LLM reads those things and generates something like, "The most likely cause is a mismatch in the pair mapping introduced by the latest configuration update." Then it might recommend, "Review these three fields, compare them with the last known successful configuration, and then run this validation before resubmitting." Notice that everything specific in that answer, the fields, the last good configuration, the validation, it all came from what was retrieved. >> So, you're saying the model is not supposed to invent that answer. >> Exactly. The goal is to ground the answer in retrieved enterprise information, not in the model's imagination. And that's where rules come in. And I keep hammering this home in every single episode that we do, but I it simply can't be overstated enough. The power of the model is usually where the least of your issues lie, and it tends to be where fixes aren't needed. It is always in the framework you build around it. It's in the rules. It's in giving it only the context it needs so that it follows those rules without hallucinating over large amounts of context. And that's what we really work to do in Case Resolver was to make sure it gets just the information it needs, that it's fast, it doesn't have to run some gigantic model that's going to take forever to run an answer because the framework around it is so robust, it doesn't need to. >> All right, big question for you here, Alec. Does RAG actually solve hallucinations? >> No, RAG in itself is not the solution to hallucinations, and that's one of the biggest misconceptions. Just grounding it isn't enough, but RAG does improve grounding. It doesn't guarantee correctness. You can retrieve the wrong information. You can retrieve outdated information. And you can retrieve just incomplete information. Going back to chunking, so that you might have cut off something that you needed. And the LLM can still mis- misunderstand what you retrieved. There are many possible failure points for chunking, bad retrieval, outdated knowledge, weak metadata, too many irrelevant results, like too too little relevant information, bad prompts, and ambiguous documentation. And the hardest one to catch is a confident answer built on a stale document, because it reads exactly like a correct one. And the model's going to come back completely confident and say this is the answer, and you're not going to know what happened. So, having clean data and I feel like a broken record saying this all the time, good framework is important. So, a framework that that tells the model, "Hey, this document over here is outdated. This one has been replaced. This one is 10 years old." Providing a framework so that the model obtains the right information is so important. >> Right. So, adding on to what uh Lakshay were saying, not only rules, but also having some ways to figuring out the documentation that you have, the how much weightage do we give on those or the quality of the documentation itself. Going back to your original point, like when you look at hallucination, that's where the testing and evaluation is so important. You need to test three different uh type of questions or scenarios multiple times, right? Or multiple test cases for those. One is, do we retrieve the right information? Did the model interpret the information correctly? And lastly, and did the recommendation actually help the help solve the case quicker than what otherwise I would have done? >> Yeah. Okay, so guys, let's move on to agents because lately everything seems to be described as an AI agent. And so, tell me what is an agent in practical terms. >> So, I love agents, but and it it in early on in AI, it seemed like everyone was just rushing to make bigger and bigger models with more parameters, larger data centers, that'll solve everything. But now, everyone's realizing that the power from it comes in this developing agentic systems. So, to answer your question, an agent is a system that can do more than just simply generate a response. It can decide which steps to take, it can use tools, it can retrieve information, it can call APIs, it can invoke workflows, and it can potentially perform multiple steps towards a goal. And this is genuinely the most important and fastest developing space in AI right now. If you look at Claude code, code x, every single company is just racing to build the best agentic framework possible and that's where all the resources are going because that's where people find actual tangible use in AI rather than just getting a text response. >> Okay, then what actually separates that from a like that agent from a chatbot? >> A chatbot just primarily responds to text output. An agent can reason and it can take its output and act on it. That's what's important. >> And that distinction is important. So, let's go through an example, Clint. Suppose a customer says I can't access a feature I paid for. A chatbot might explain how to access the feature, how it's supposed to work, but the agent could potentially check whether the customer has the right settings, if they do they have the entitlement set up right, do we have any prior cases that had similar complaint, is the customer payment is past due, whatever the case may be. It basically goes through one uh problem identification after another and then it can identify the problem problem and trigger if there is a solution, if you have configured it to do an action, a workflow, it will execute on that workflow. It can update the case and it can also respond to the customer about the resolution or the next step. So, it can do it all like a human does. We basically have moved from answering to res- resolving. That's where that's the distinction from chatbot to agent. >> Now, as the agent gets smarter, does a smarter mo- model actually mean a better agent? >> No, not necessarily. And agents depend heavily on the tools you give them and their ability to call tools is important, too. The framework has always is the most important part and you'll actually find that some of the the most reliable and useful and cheap models out there are actually open source open weights models you could install on your PC right now. You can run it on consumer hardware. It's not that huge, but it's so reliable with tool calling that it's useful as an agent. It's really strong as an agent. An example is the Quen line of models. And they need reliable APIs in their framework, reliable actions, reliable queries, permissions, workflow integration. If all the tools that you hand them are weak, the agent will be weak. So, building out a tool belt for it is really important, too. It's like a brilliant chef with a really smart agent is like a brilliant chef, but it has a broken stove and it still serves a bad meal, no matter how good the chef is. And every tool you hand an agent is also a permission. If it can update a record, you have to be comfortable with what happens when it updates that record wrong. So, as always, the framework you give it, it's all that matters. >> And that's why enterprise AI architecture will matter, you guys. The LLM we know is the most visible part, but the real operation comes from connecting intelligence that's available in different enterprise systems. It's not just, you know, what you see in the front with LLM. >> Okay, and how do rag and agents fit together? >> They actually fit very naturally. It's a wonderful pairing. And a simple way to think about it is rag helps the agent know things. Tools help the agent do things. And imagine a support agent receives a case. It retrieves similar cases and relevant knowledge. That part is the rag. Then it decides, I need to verify this customer's subscription, so it will call an API. That's the tool belt. Then I should check whether there's a known outage. It calls the monitoring system. Then I need to update the case and create a follow-up task. It performs those actions. That's the agent workflow. It retrieves all the information it needs. It uses tools to access things outside that it doesn't have on hand, And that creates a really capable autonomous worker. >> So the So the retrieval provides context. The agent provides orchestration and actions. The combination of the two where is a lot of practical value comes from. So, they both fit naturally and they need to come together to provide value. >> And I'm sure those are listening they're probably wondering like how does this all fit into Salesforce? >> And I'd say Salesforce again, I've said that before I'm just going to say they've done a good job bringing all the pieces together under Salesforce. In trust that tools available. The operational context is already there, right? So you already know customer information, you already know cases, knowledge, entitlement, permissions, flows, whatever business intelligence that you want to decode is already there in your CRM. So with platform capabilities that they've added to Agent Force, AI agents can increasingly operate directly within this workflow. But most enterprises also have important information outside Salesforce. Now that's where it gets tricky. So you might have an agent operating inside Salesforce, but it uses retrieval external. It relies on retrieving information from outside from a vector database. Or you may have AI services sitting outside and interacting with Salesforce to do a business flows. So, it's not just everything is within Salesforce as the truth with enterprise. >> So again, it doesn't have to be one single architecture then. >> Exactly. And we had this discussion earlier in one of our episodes where we said and this is our experience. Smaller, less complex organizations with fewer systems, it can be Salesforce. Larger organizations, definitely a hybrid approach. >> All right, let's challenge the hype then. Does every enterprise AI project need a vector database? >> Definitely not. And I think when developing architectures as a general rule, it's important to not have a one-shoe-fits-all policy. There's always going to be a level of tailoring that's needed. So, in this case, if the information is structured and easy to query, just use a normal structured search on a database. If you need the account balance, the case status, entitlement level, or order number, you want a database query because that information is predictable, easy to sort, easy to find. And that's the benefit of a database. But, what it doesn't capture is semantic similarity. When things are nuanced, when things are unpredictable, where it has to capture exactly the details around a specific situation, vector search like it it excels there because it adds that nuance. And vector search also isn't free. It's another reason why you shouldn't default to it. Every document has to be embedded and re-embedded every time it changes. Think of the cost that adds latency. And vector search becomes much more useful with that unstructured information. The documents, the case notes, emails, all of that stuff. >> Right. A common mistake is using vector search for everything simply because it sounds advanced. That would be I could see the hype and people want to show that they're meeting their objective for the year. They got vector database and they got vector search available for different use cases. My advice is to use the simplest technology that reliably solves your problem. It doesn't even have to be AI and we advocate for that. If you can solve some problem through deterministic rules, that's the right solution. >> Okay, let me ask this. Can you combine traditional and semantic search? >> Yes. It's called hybrid search and often you should. It's the blend of that really captures both of the the strengths of both and shores up each other's weaknesses. You might use semantic search to find related historical cases, then fill then filter them by product, version, customer type, date. That's often much better than semantic similarity by itself. Just don't filter so hard that you hide the one older case that actually had the answer you were looking for. So, metadata becomes extremely important. When was the document created? What version does it apply to? Is it approved? These are all details that need to be used as filtration systems that give the AI the correct contents in the relevant context cuz it won't know the difference. It'll answer confidently. Metadata's the label on a jar stating what it's for and whether it's past its expiration date. And that's what really makes this hybrid search powerful and it's what we did with Case Resolver. It's the blend that brings out the magic. >> And you talked about the metadata, right? So, if you see a lot of these AI projects, eventually expose data governance problems because they rely on that. The quality of AI solution depends on the quality of the the data underneath. The information that it has underneath, yeah. >> Okay, so how do you actually test this? >> So, to test this, you test retrieval separately from generation. So, first, you just test if we retrieve the right information. Second, you test did the model use that information correctly? And third, did the answer actually solve the problem? If the answer was wrong, you need to know where it failed. Was the knowledge wrong? Or was the model wrong? You don't need a huge research project for this either. A set of real cases where you already know the right answer really goes a long way here. When we tuned Case Resolver's similarity cutoff, we tested retrieval on its own, and then we measured where the real and unrelated matches scored on our test data, and then we drew the line between them. >> Ultimately, you also need to go back to your business metrics. Did case resolution improve? Did the agent accept the recommendations? Did the escalations numbers have have the escalation numbers have gone down? Did the case remain result. That's what really matters. >> Okay, one more buzzword. Does agentic automatically mean autonomous? >> No, and that distinction's very important for the tuning process. An agent can recommend an action, it can prepare an action, it can ask for approval, or it can act automatically. Those are all different levels of permissions and autonomy. Think of it as like a dimmer switch, not an off on-off switch. And that matters because it needs to build trust. You need to understand what the system is good at. And you can gradually build permissions as you go. So, when you start with one of these projects, you probably don't want actions to be autonomous. You want to understand the system. Where is it returning really reliable answers that you'll never have to worry about? Maybe there it can take autonomous actions. You should separate between actions that you can't take back, like automatically sending an email to a customer. That's not something you can undo or take back. If that's wrong, that that's on you. But maybe updating a field in a database, that can easily be rolled back and is lower risk. >> Enterprises should move through through these level gradually. You start with assistance, you go with recommendation next then action with approval, and then selectively, as Alec was alluding to, selectively autonomy where the risk and confidence justify that. >> Okay, let's connect this directly to Case Resolver then. How does Rez use these concepts? >> The problem we are solving is case resolution. When a case comes in, Rez needs to understand what is the issue, have we seen it before, what knowledge applies, do we have any customer information around it, do we have knowledge articles on this particular topic? So, all of that information information we gather, and then we decide what should happen next. That's where the semantics search and retrieval becomes useful for us. >> And taking a peek under the hood here, Rez blends data cloud semantic search with keyword search, and it respects Salesforce permissions on every record it pulls. That's another level of trust and security. And then once we have enough context, the system can then start helping with action. It can draft a response, create a follow-up task, recommend an an escalation, or trigger a workflow. Some of that is already there. Rez recommends when to escalate, draft an email, and a call script. A person reviews everything before it goes out. It's that human step that matters there for those important actions. And Rez ships as an action that a customer's own agent or flow can call. So, retrieval and agentic capabilities, they both support different parts of the resolution process. >> And I don't want customer to care whether we technically call something rag or agentic. They should care that the case gets resolved faster and more consistently. And if I may add on, economically, right, financially viable options as well. >> All right, guys. So, give me the hype versus reality version of this. >> The hype is add an M&M, add a rag, add a vector database, add an agent, add an agent studio. The reality is So, that's all hype, and we've gone through it chasing it for last 2 years. The reality is that you need good knowledge, good retrieval, good system integration, good workflows, good governance, good data, and a business problem worth solving, and you know how to measure the solution. >> And most failures are not because the model isn't smart enough. Again, if I can just slide my catchphrase in here again, it's the framework that matters. They have The failures happen because context, tools, data, or the evaluation are weak. >> All right, guys. You know what time it is. It is rapid fire. I'm going to ask some short questions or short I want short answers. I'm going to ask quick questions, short answers. Retrieve them. Tell you I'm watching the clock this time. >> Understood. >> That usually means three minute answers. >> All right, so rag or fine-tuning? >> For enterprise knowledge, I would say rag first. >> Especially for frequently changing information. >> All right, vector database or traditional database? >> Use the right one for the data. I'll answer that way. >> I would sort it by structured data, use a traditional database. If it has semantic knowledge >> wondering you need to know the situation, use vector database. >> All right, how about embeddings in one sentence? >> Numbers that represent meaning. >> Yeah, I don't know enough, so I'll defer it to Alec on this one. >> [laughter] >> All right, biggest rag mistake. >> Thinking more data automatically means better answers. >> Poor retrieval quality, I would say. Giving the data something that has an answer confidently wrongly. >> All right, biggest agent mistake. >> Too much authority too early. >> I would say weak tools so that it it can't really take any important actions or and guardrails. >> All right, does every AI app need a vector database? >> No. >> No, absolutely not. >> All right, keyword search or semantic search? >> I will go with both as Alec said earlier. Stick with him on that. >> Hybrid where appropriate. If there's absolutely no semantics in what you're reading, then maybe only one. >> All right. Which is more important, model quality or context quality? >> Uh context, context. >> Definitely context. It Input bad input means bad output. >> And can rag eliminate hallucinations? >> No. >> It can reduce the risk, yes. Eliminate it, no. And if improperly done, it can make way worse. >> Can an agent be useful without autonomy? >> Absolutely. Yeah, they can cut the resolution time quite a bit. >> And yeah, I'd say most enterprise agents should start here. >> I Curve Ball, what matters more in support, answering or acting? >> I would say dissolving. >> I would say just acting correctly. >> All right, most underrated part of rag. >> One thing I learned from Alex on this call, metadata. >> I'd say evaluation. >> All right, finish this sentence. An AI agent is useful when >> when it moves the case closer to the solution. >> I'd say when it has the right context and safe tools. >> Rag, agents, and vector databases in three words. >> I would say context, the action, recommendation. >> I'd say retrieve, reason, and act. >> All right, thanks, guys. That's probably the simplest way to wrap this up. Rag helps AI find the right information. Vector databases help retrieve information by meaning. And then agents use tools and workflows to take action. And LLMs, they help interpret, reason, and generate. But none of those technologies create business value by itself. Rajiv, any final thoughts? >> Yes, and this would be a repeat of what I've said earlier in different episode. Start with the service problem, don't start with the architecture diagram. Don't chase the technology. What are your agents or users struggling with? What information do they keep repeatedly search for? What cases keep getting escalated? What action could safely be automated? Then decide whether rag, semantic search, agents, or vector database actually helps solve those problems. The technology should follow the business use case. >> All right, Alex, how about you? >> I'd say from a technical standpoint, keep the system understandable. Know what was retrieved. Know what the model saw. Know which tool was called. Know why an action happened. Auditability here is key because these systems are always going to be imperfect upon first implementation. There's this saying that code never survives its first exposure to the real world. And that tuning matters and knowing where to tune is important. And all of that knowledge and logging helps with that. In Case Resolver, that shows with that starts with showing support agents the past cases behind every suggestion and keeping a record of every attempt and how it turned out. The more capable a system becomes, the more important that visibility becomes. >> Um I think that's a great place to wrap up. Rajiv and Alex, thanks again and thanks everyone for listening to another episode of Beyond the Case. We'll see you next time. >> Thank you, Clint.

metadata.title: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
metadata.author: IBM Technology
metadata.shortDescription:
Ready to become a certified GenAI engineer? Register now and use code IBMTechYT20 for 20% off of your exam → https://ibm.biz/BdGhCF
Learn about the technology → https://ibm.biz/BdMsRT

Large language models usually give great answers, but because they're limited to the training data used to create the model. Over time they can become incomplete--or worse, generate answers that are just plain wrong. One way of improving the LLM results is called "retrieval-augmented generation" or RAG. In this video, IBM Senior Research Scientist Marina Danilevsky explains the LLM/RAG framework and how this combination delivers two big advantages, namely: the model gets the most up-to-date and trustworthy facts, and you can see where the model got its info, lending more credibility to what it generates.

segments.text: Large language models. They are everywhere.
They get some things amazingly right
and other things very interestingly wrong.
My name is Marina Danilevsky.
I am a Senior Research Scientist here at IBM Research.
And I want to tell you about a framework to help large language models
be more accurate and more up to date:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG.
Let's just talk about the "Generation" part for a minute.
So forget the "Retrieval-Augmented".
So the generation, this refers to large language models, or LLMs,
that generate text in response to a user query, referred to as a prompt.
These models can have some undesirable behavior.
I want to tell you an anecdote to illustrate this.
So my kids, they recently asked me this question:
"In our solar system, what planet has the most moons?"
And my response was, “Oh, that's really great that you're asking this question. I loved space when I was your age.”
Of course, that was like 30 years ago.
But I know this! I read an article
and the article said that it was Jupiter and 88 moons. So that's the answer.
Now, actually, there's a couple of things wrong with my answer.
First of all, I have no source to support what I'm saying.
So even though I confidently said “I read an article, I know the answer!”, I'm not sourcing it.
I'm giving the answer off the top of my head.
And also, I actually haven't kept up with this for awhile, and my answer is out of date.
So we have two problems here. One is no source. And the second problem is that I am out of date.
And these, in fact, are two behaviors that are often observed as problematic
when interacting with large language models. They’re LLM challenges.
Now, what would have happened if I'd taken a beat and first gone
and looked up the answer on a reputable source like NASA?
Well, then I would have been able to say, “Ah, okay! So the answer is Saturn with 146 moons.”
And in fact, this keeps changing because scientists keep on discovering more and more moons.
So I have now grounded my answer in something more believable.
I have not hallucinated or made up an answer.
Oh, by the way, I didn't leak personal information about how long ago it's been since I was obsessed with space.
All right, so what does this have to do with large language models?
Well, how would a large language model have answered this question?
So let's say that I have a user asking this question about moons.
A large language model would confidently say,
OK, I have been trained and from what I know in my parameters during my training, the answer is Jupiter.
The answer is wrong. But, you know, we don't know.
The large language model is very confident in what it answered.
Now, what happens when you add this retrieval augmented part here?
What does that mean?
That means that now, instead of just relying on what the LLM knows,
we are adding a content store.
This could be open like the internet.
This can be closed like some collection of documents, collection of policies, whatever.
The point, though, now is that the LLM first goes and talks
to the content store and says, “Hey, can you retrieve for me
information that is relevant to what the user's query was?”
And now, with this retrieval-augmented answer, it's not Jupiter anymore.
We know that it is Saturn. What does this look like?
Well, first user prompts the LLM with their question.
They say, this is what my question was.
And originally, if we're just talking to a generative model,
the generative model says, “Oh, okay, I know the response. Here it is. Here's my response.”
But now in the RAG framework,
the generative model actually has an instruction that says, "No, no, no."
"First, go and retrieve relevant content."
"Combine that with the user's question and only then generate the answer."
So the prompt now has three parts:
the instruction to pay attention to, the retrieved content, together with the user's question.
Now give a response. And in fact, now you can give evidence for why your response was what it was.
So now hopefully you can see, how does RAG help the two LLM challenges that I had mentioned before?
So first of all, I'll start with the out of date part.
Now, instead of having to retrain your model, if new information comes up, like,
hey, we found some more moons-- now to Jupiter again, maybe it'll be Saturn again in the future.
All you have to do is you augment your data store with new information, update information.
So now the next time that a user comes and asks the question, we're ready.
We just go ahead and retrieve the most up to date information.
The second problem, source.
Well, the large language model is now being instructed to pay attention
to primary source data before giving its response.
And in fact, now being able to give evidence.
This makes it less likely to hallucinate or to leak data
because it is less likely to rely only on information that it learned during training.
It also allows us to get the model to have a behavior that can be very positive,
which is knowing when to say, “I don't know.”
If the user's question cannot be reliably answered based on your data store,
the model should say, "I don't know," instead of making up something that is believable and may mislead the user.
This can have a negative effect as well though, because if the retriever is not sufficiently good
to give the large language model the best, most high-quality grounding information,
then maybe the user's query that is answerable doesn't get an answer.
So this is actually why lots of folks, including many of us here at IBM,
are working the problem on both sides.
We are both working to improve the retriever
to give the large language model the best quality data on which to ground its response,
and also the generative part so that the LLM can give the richest, best response finally to the user
when it generates the answer.
Thank you for learning more about RAG and like and subscribe to the channel.
Thank you.

I'm giving the answer off the top of my head. And also, I actually haven't kept up with this for awhile, and my answer is out of date. So we have two problems here. One is no source. And the second problem is that I am out of date. And these, in fact, are two behaviors that are often observed as problematic when interacting with large language models. They’re LLM challenges. Now, what would have happened if I'd taken a beat and first gone and looked up the answer on a reputable source like NASA? Well, then I would have been able to say, “Ah, okay! So the answer is Saturn with 146 moons.” And in fact, this keeps changing because scientists keep on discovering more and more moons. So I have now grounded my answer in something more believable. I have not hallucinated or made up an answer. Oh, by the way, I didn't leak personal information about how long ago it's been since I was obsessed with space. All right, so what does this have to do with large language models? Well, how would a large language model have answered this question? So let's say that I have a user asking this question about moons. A large language model would confidently say, OK, I have been trained and from what I know in my parameters during my training, the answer is Jupiter. The answer is wrong. But, you know, we don't know. The large language model is very confident in what it answered. Now, what happens when you add this retrieval augmented part here? What does that mean? That means that now, instead of just relying on what the LLM knows, we are adding a content store. This could be open like the internet. This can be closed like some collection of documents, collection of policies, whatever. The point, though, now is that the LLM first goes and talks to the content store and says, “Hey, can you retrieve for me information that is relevant to what the user's query was?” And now, with this retrieval-augmented answer, it's not Jupiter anymore. We know that it is Saturn. What does this look like? Well, first user prompts the LLM with their question. They say, this is what my question was. And originally, if we're just talking to a generative model, the generative model says, “Oh, okay, I know the response. Here it is. Here's my response.” But now in the RAG framework, the generative model actually has an instruction that says, "No, no, no." "First, go and retrieve relevant content." "Combine that with the user's question and only then generate the answer." So the prompt now has three parts: the instruction to pay attention to, the retrieved content, together with the user's question. Now give a response. And in fact, now you can give evidence for why your response was what it was. So now hopefully you can see, how does RAG help the two LLM challenges that I had mentioned before? So first of all, I'll start with the out of date part. Now, instead of having to retrain your model, if new information comes up, like, hey, we found some more moons-- now to Jupiter again, maybe it'll be Saturn again in the future. All you have to do is you augment your data store with new information, update information. So now the next time that a user comes and asks the question, we're ready. We just go ahead and retrieve the most up to date information. The second problem, source. Well, the large language model is now being instructed to pay attention to primary source data before giving its response. And in fact, now being able to give evidence. This makes it less likely to hallucinate or to leak data because it is less likely to rely only on information that it learned during training. It also allows us to get the model to have a behavior that can be very positive, which is knowing when to say, “I don't know.” If the user's question cannot be reliably answered based on your data store, the model should say, "I don't know," instead of making up something that is believable and may mislead the user. This can have a negative effect as well though, because if the retriever is not sufficiently good to give the large language model the best, most high-quality grounding information, then maybe the user's query that is answerable doesn't get an answer. So this is actually why lots of folks, including many of us here at IBM, are working the problem on both sides. We are both working to improve the retriever to give the large language model the best quality data on which to ground its response, and also the generative part so that the LLM can give the richest, best response finally to the user when it generates the answer. Thank you for learning more about RAG and like and subscribe to the channel. Thank you.

metadata.title: The Future of Enterprise AI: RAG vs. Agentic Workflows
metadata.author: Hey sidG
metadata.shortDescription:
Most businesses have started their AI journey with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)—essentially giving AI a "memory" of company data. But is a well-informed "librarian" enough for your enterprise? In this video, we explore the strategic shift from knowledge to action: the move toward Agentic AI.

[Key Takeaways]

The Knowledge Gap: Why general-purpose AI often "hallucinates" and how to ground it in your private business data.

The First Leap (RAG): How RAG reduces hallucinations by 70-90% and builds foundational trust.

The Next Frontier (Agents): Moving beyond information recall to autonomous systems that can reason, decide, and act.

Agentic RAG: The hybrid model that combines the best of both worlds for a 171% average ROI in sectors like Finance and Healthcare.

Strategic Choice: Should your AI simply tell you something, or do something for you?

[Call to Action]
Is your organization ready to make the leap from a knowledgeable AI to an actionable one? Let us know in the comments how you're implementing agents in your workflow!

#generativeai  #agenticai  #enterpriseai  #RAG  #machinelearning  #aistrategy  #notebooklm  #digitaltransformation  #futureofwork  #aiautomation

metadata.title: Open WebUI Knowledge Bases: RAG & Embeddings (Beginner's Guide)
metadata.author: Professor Patterns
metadata.shortDescription:
How AI Actually "Understands" words : https://youtu.be/ITsy52sV0oM?si=-PrgeHhOm9X-n6IR


Unlock the power of modern document search with this comprehensive guide to Knowledge Bases in Open WebUI. Learn how to leverage RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) and embedding models to transform your document management experience. Through a practical example of resume screening, discover how these technologies work together to make document search more intelligent and efficient.

In this tutorial, we explore:
Setting up Knowledge Bases in Open WebUI
Understanding embedding models and their role in document processing
Configuring RAG templates for optimal results
Practical implementation with real-world resume screening
Advanced features including hybrid search and re-ranking models

Perfect for developers, technical managers, and anyone interested in implementing modern document search solutions. Whether you're new to RAG systems or looking to optimize your existing setup, this guide provides clear, actionable insights into building effective knowledge management systems.

🔧 Technical Stack Covered:
Open WebUI
Sentence Transformers
Embedding Models
RAG Architecture
Document Processing

⭐️ Links mentioned in the video:
SBERT.net: https://sbert.net/
Hugging Face Models: https://huggingface.co/models?library=sentence-transformers&sort=downloads

metadata.title: Webinar: How to Build Enterprise-Ready RAG Systems
metadata.author: Unstructured
metadata.shortDescription:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), in all its diverse forms, is quickly becoming the backbone of enterprise AI systems, enabling organizations to combine the reasoning power of large language models with the context of their own data. But moving from proof-of-concept to production takes more than just plugging in a vector database. It requires thoughtful planning around security, data governance, and performance evaluation.

In this webinar, we explored what it took to implement RAG at enterprise scale—covering the technical foundations, organizational alignment, and practical methods for evaluating and improving system quality over time. We also discussed how enterprises were measuring success by focusing on end-user experience and business outcomes, ensuring that AI solutions didn’t just work, but delivered real value.

In this session, we walked through:
- How to secure enterprise RAG deployments and manage sensitive data access
- Strategies for continuous evaluation (Evals) to maintain quality and reduce hallucinations
- How RAG systems were helping employees tackle complex, high-value business problems
- How RAG was being leveraged by Agentic Systems

metadata.author: Cresco International
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you make AI answer questions using your company's own data instead of relying only on what it learned during training?

In this video, we explain Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the architecture powering the next generation of enterprise AI.

You'll learn:
🔹 What RAG is and how it works
🔹 The 7-step RAG architecture explained
🔹 Document ingestion, embeddings, retrieval, and generation
🔹 How vector databases like Pinecone and Weaviate enable semantic search
🔹 Why RAG reduces hallucinations and improves AI accuracy
🔹 A practical implementation roadmap for enterprise AI

📊 Key Industry Insights
• 78% of organizations use AI in at least one business function (McKinsey).
• Retrieval-based AI is becoming the preferred architecture for enterprise GenAI applications.
• Modern vector databases can retrieve relevant information from millions of embeddings in under 50 milliseconds.

Whether you're an AI enthusiast, data engineer, IT leader, architect, or business executive, this video provides a clear introduction to one of the most important technologies shaping enterprise AI today.

🌐 Learn more about Cresco International:

metadata.title: Every RAG Strategy Explained in 13 Minutes (No Fluff)
metadata.author: Cole Medin
metadata.shortDescription:
Retrieval Augmented Generation is THE way to give your AI agents the ability to search and leverage your documents and knowledge. But there are a million strategies for RAG out there - how do you know what is ideal for your use case? What even are all of the RAG strategies I can pick from? Should I combine some together?

I've got you covered with all of these questions in this video. Beware this is very informationally dense, but it'll get you started thinking about what strategies to apply to your use cases. 

Also let me know in the comments which RAG strategies you want me to cover more on my channel!

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

- If you want to master AI coding assistants and learn how to build systems for reliable and repeatable results, check out the new Agentic Coding Course in Dynamous:
https://dynamous.ai/agentic-coding-course

- Neon is the Postgres platform I used to showcase real RAG data: check it out here:
https://get.neon.com/jR4SxEE

- Here is the repo that outlines all the RAG strategies with examples:
https://github.com/coleam00/ottomator-agents/tree/main/all-rag-strategies

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

00:00 - Intro: The Importance of RAG
01:08 - RAG Explained in 1 Minute
02:22 - Resources for Each RAG Strategy
02:51 - RAG Strategy #1 - Reranking
03:46 - RAG Strategy #2 - Agentic RAG (includes Hybrid Search)
04:42 - RAG Strategy #3 - Knowledge Graphs
05:33 - RAG Strategy #4 - Contextual Retrieval
06:26 - RAG Strategy #5 - Query Expansion
06:56 - RAG Strategy #6 - Multi-Query RAG
07:22 - RAG Strategy #7 - Context-Aware Chunking
08:20 - RAG Strategy #8 - Late Chunking
09:08 - RAG Strategy #9 - Hierarchical RAG (Using Metadata)
10:15 - RAG Strategy #10 - Self-Reflective RAG
10:51 - RAG Strategy #11 - Fine-tuned Embeddings
12:00 - Final Thoughts

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Join me as I push the limits of what is possible with AI. I'll be uploading videos weekly - at least every Wednesday at 7:00 PM CDT!

segments.text: Let's look at modern boutique agencies.
They often pull in high six-figure gross
revenues, yet the net profit they
actually take home is disproportionately
small. This massive bleed in
profitability rarely comes down to a
lack of technical skill or poor
execution on the deliverables
themselves. This chart illustrates where
that money actually goes. Starting with
a $250,000 gross margin at the top, we
see segments breaking away. Hours burned
chasing delayed client assets, unmanaged
revision loops, out-of-hours
communication, and vague decision rates
eating up unbilled time. Treating a
project delivery as a purely isolated
transaction, rather than the foundation
of an ongoing relationship, guarantees
this exact cycle of margin erosion. High
margin retention depends on a foundation
of rigid operational engineering.
Solving this requires the implementation
of visible, non-negotiable operational
gates that enforce boundaries from the
exact moment the deposit invoice clears.
Without an operational layer dictating
the terms of engagement, an agency
effectively surrenders its profit
margins to the unpredictable behavioral
quirks of every new client. In
high-ticket B2B engagements, client
excitement does not peak during project
delivery. It peaks during the sales
negotiation, when they are visualizing
the solution. But the instant a large
deposit invoice clears a client's bank
account, their psychology shifts. They
have relinquished financial liquidity,
yet they possess zero tangible work
product in return. This graph tracks the
psychological timeline. The blue line is
sales dopamine. At deposit paid,
dopamine plummets. A second line for
anxiety spikes into the red post-payment
void. If an agency goes silent during
the 72-hour window, the client's
narrative sours. Anxiety breeds
skepticism and micromanagement. The
countermeasure to this anxiety is the
120-minute protocol. Within 2 hours of
payment, the agency must systematically
dispatch a formal payment confirmation,
a comprehensive eight-part welcome
packet, and a direct kickoff scheduling
link.
The welcome packet explicitly sets the
rules of engagement before production
ever starts. It documents official
communication channels, expected
response turnaround times, and strict
revision limits.
This immediate structured barrage of
onboarding material replaces the
client's vulnerability with deep
confidence in the agency's operational
authority.
Whoever controls the narrative in the
first 72 hours dictates the power
dynamics for the remainder of the
engagement.
Amateur service providers treat client
intake as a generic administrative
questionnaire.
High-performing studios treat it as a
risk management diagnostic. This
requires a 30-question diagnostic
intake, which the client must complete
within 48 hours of onboarding. The
single most critical requirement in this
intake is forcing the client
organization to officially designate
exactly one authorized sign-off lead.
Without this, you invite the consensus
committee, a toxic behavioral pattern
where multiple stakeholders provide
contradictory feedback, paralyzing all
decision-making. Mandating a single
sign-off lead up front neutralizes this
threat before it can derail a milestone,
creating clear, single-point
accountability.
The intake must also be used to extract
all technical dependencies, server
credentials, and master brand assets
immediately into a secure vault.
Once assets are secured and the kickoff
is complete, active production begins
under the fast win principle. The fast
win principle requires the agency to
deliver one small, but highly visible
and tangible artifact within the first
seven business days. This could be a
competitor benchmark, an executive
opportunity heat map, or an interactive
wireframe. The goal is not to finish the
project early, but to prove immediate
forward momentum.
By combining rigid technical extraction
with a rapid visible win, the agency
eliminates the client's urge to
micromanage the execution phase. As the
project progresses, scope creep is
inevitable. However, margin loss
resulting from that scope creep is
entirely optional.
This diagram shows a scope fence matrix.
It demonstrates that what is explicitly
excluded from a project must be made
just as visible as what is included,
creating clear boundaries for
deliverables like a web build or brand
system.
To prevent clients from stalling this
momentum, the agency must enforce a
strict 48-hour feedback SLA. This is
enforced through the day-for-day slip
clause. If the client delays asset
delivery or milestone approvals, the
final project deadline automatically
extends by the exact same number of
days. When a client inevitably requests
out of scope work, simply telling them
no creates immediate defensive friction.
Instead, validate the idea and offer a
clear commercial choice. Option A logs
the request into a phase two backlog,
while option B prices the change and
adjusts the current schedule. This logic
forms the basis of the 12 script
communication armory, a system designed
to handle boundary tests and delays
without draining your emotional energy.
For example, if a client sends a project
request to a personal mobile device on a
Sunday evening, the script dictates you
never reply via text. You redirect the
message into the official project portal
to be reviewed during standard business
hours. Documented scripts and visible
matrices turn scope control into a
mathematical certainty. Traditional
pitches for recurring retainers usually
fail because they are introduced at the
very end of a project, making them feel
like a discretionary last-minute sales
ask. Client retention is actually a
60-day operational engine that must be
built while the core project is still
being delivered. Step one of this engine
triggers at day 21 with the value
snapshot. This is a concise executive
memo documenting the unexpected
technical risks your team neutralized
and early positive metrics. It
intentionally asks for zero money
establishing strategic indispensability
early on. Step two triggers at day 45
with the quarterly business review. The
QBR is used to pivot the relationship
dynamic from deliverable execution to
ongoing growth advisory by presenting an
evidence-based gap analysis. This chart
visualizes the economic anchor formula
used to present the retainer price. By
anchoring a $3,500 monthly retainer
against the massive cost of a $75,000
full-time senior hire, the value of the
agency's ongoing efficiency becomes
obvious.
By making the agency's value explicitly
legible throughout the project, the
transition to a recurring retainer
becomes the logical operational next
step rather than a separate high
friction purchase decision. The entire
client retention operating system
functions as a unified 60-day
chronological checklist spanning from
the very first payment all the way to
the retainer transition.
Implementing this begins by loading the
30-question diagnostic into a form tool
and making the single sign-off lead a
mandatory field. Next, customize the
welcome packet to clearly define your
true response times and communication
boundaries. Finally, hardcode the
three-column scope fence matrix directly
into all future standard statements of
work. These operational tools take less
than one afternoon to deploy, but they
will instantly protect the profit
margins of your very next client
engagement. Scaling a profitable service
business is impossible if you constantly
rely on personal heroics. True freedom
requires replacing your anxiety with
non-negotiable operational gates.

metadata.title: The $12.4K Scope Creep Killing Your Best Jobs (Fix Inside)
metadata.author: The Contractor AI | AI Systems for Contractors
metadata.shortDescription:
The average contractor loses $12.4K per $100K residential job to scope creep. 68% eat $25K a year in unbilled change orders, and don't even track it.

In this training, we broke down the  the 5-step system to stop scope creep, fast-track change orders, and hit 50-60% margins on every CO. Built for contractors sick of finding out at the end of the job that "the losing project" was actually 6 change orders they never billed.

What you'll learn:
✅ The 3 client-squeeze signals every contractor misses
✅ Why your contract is a tool, not a piece of paper
✅ The 30-second script that turns "while you're here…" into a signed CO
✅ How to go from verbal request → signed change order in under 60 minutes
✅ Why the project manager owns the CO, not the salesperson

📅 Free live training every Thursday at 3 PM ET
🎯 Book a free game plan call: https://thecontractor.ai/book-call
👥 Join the Skool community: https://www.skool.com/thecontractoraiaccelerator/about

metadata.shortDescription:
The client Slack’d “one more thing.” Last time you ate it for free.

Quiet scope-creep loop (2026):
1) Notion — freeze the original SOW and log every change
2) Claude — draft a clear change-order email + price options from your notes
3) Wave — estimate or invoice the approved add-on
Then YOU hit send. No auto-send. No contract theater.

Demo client is fictional (Northline Press Co.). No invented win rates. Not legal, contract, or tax advice.

metadata.title: Custom Software Development Pitfalls: Scope Creep, AI Dependence, and Uncapped API Costs
metadata.author: Bryan Taylor
metadata.shortDescription:
#appdevelopment   #ScopeCreep #TechDebt #SoftwareBudgeting #startuptech 

Building custom applications without a structured roadmap often leads to severe financial and operational pitfalls. Unplanned features lead to scope creep and technical debt. 

Hidden costs in hosting, AI token price inflation, and automated API messaging (like Twilio or SendGrid) can cause budget meltdowns overnight. Without strict compliance safeguards and early admin reporting tools, companies risk massive regulatory fines and bandwidth overage costs.

custom software development pitfalls, scope creep, technical debt, software budgeting, API cost management, AI coding dependencies, software compliance guardrails, bandwidth cost optimization, admin reporting tools

metadata.shortDescription:
Why AI projects creep faster than ordinary software, and the one outcome, one owner, one date rule that keeps a first AI win shipping on time.

Two members of the Augusto team talk it through in 19 minutes.

Read the full post: https://augusto.digital/insights/blogs/scope-creep-ai-projects-hold-the-line/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=podcast&utm_campaign=augusto_podcast&utm_content=ep17
Episode page: https://augusto.digital/insights/podcasts/ep-17-stopping-ai-scope-creep/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=podcast&utm_campaign=augusto_podcast&utm_content=ep17
Talk to us about your AI roadmap: https://augusto.digital/contact-augusto-digital/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=podcast&utm_campaign=augusto_podcast&utm_content=ep17

Augusto Digital. Your AI Activation Partner.

segments.text: So, I want you to picture this.
You're a leader, right? And you started
an AI project say a few months ago.
>> Yeah, full of optimism.
>> Exactly. On day one, you had this
crystal clear vision. But since that
kickoff, you've just sort of watched
this project quietly grow, I don't know,
three entirely new features.
>> Right.
>> And somewhere along the way, it just
completely lost its launch date.
If that sounds familiar, you are
absolutely not alone.
>> No, not at all. I mean, we are seeing
this exact scenario play out almost
everywhere right now across our client
work at Gusto Digital.
>> Yeah, which is exactly why we're doing
this deep dive today. We really want to
talk through our own internal thinking,

what we're actually building.
>> Because the reality on the ground is

bottomless money pits.
>> Yeah, they really do.

We're also going to explore this single
scope rule that actually holds the line.

>> Highly crucial.
And then we'll break down the five-step
checklist we actually use in our client
engagements to guarantee a shipped
product.
>> Yeah, let's get into it.
>> So, let's start with the the root of the
problem, right? Why is it so much harder
to hold the line with an AI build
compared to just a normal software
application?
>> Well, I think the best way to understand
this is to look at a scenario we
literally just walked through.
So, across the last six weeks of one AI
engagement we were running, scope creep
came up in five separate meetings.
>> Five meetings in six weeks?
>> Yeah.
And what's fascinating here is that it
wasn't like out of carelessness. No one
was actively trying to sabotage the
timeline or delay the project.
>> It was born out of pure enthusiasm,
>> wasn't it? Like the first version
worked, stakeholders saw it,
and suddenly a single demo just spawns
three entirely new requests.
>> Exactly. They look at a successful test
and they immediately ask could it also
read the invoices or, you know, could it
answer our driver's questions? Could it
just post this data directly to the
accounting system?
>> And the thing is every single one of
those requests is completely reasonable
in isolation.
>> Yeah, they make sense.
>> But when you stack them together, they
turn what should be a tightly scoped six
week first win into, well, a year-long
platform.
>> With absolutely no launch date in sight.
>> Right. I always think of traditional
software prototyping kind of like
building a cardboard architectural
model.
>> Oh yeah, that's a good way to look at
it.
>> Right. Like it takes an architect an
afternoon to build it. It looks
incredible. And a stakeholder looks at
it and thinks, wow, this house is
basically done.
>> But they don't see the plumbing.
>> Exactly. They don't see the plumbing,
the electrical, the structural
engineering, all the stuff that takes
months to actually build.
But with AI, it's fundamentally
different.
An AI prototype isn't just an empty
cardboard house.
>> No, it's it's a cardboard house with a
wild animal living inside of it.
>> Yes.
The large language model is the wild
animal. And getting the animal to do a
trick once inside the cardboard box is
easy.
>> Right, you just prompt it.
>> But building a reinforced steel cage,
you know, the integrations, the
permissions, the guard rails, all of
that so that the animal doesn't escape
and wreck your entire house, that takes
months.
>> That captures the specific danger of AI
beautifully. It creates this this
illusion of competence.
>> of competence, yeah.
>> Right, because an LLM can summarize a
document in a prototype in what, five
seconds?
>> Pretty much instantly, yeah.
>> So to a non-technical stakeholder,
extending that to 10 other systems looks
like it'll only take another five
seconds.
But the integration is where the project
just goes to die.
>> It really is.
>> I mean, if we connect this to the
broader industry, you can look at the
MIT Nanda study.
They track enterprise technology
adoption and they recently found that
95% of enterprise AI pilots deliver zero
measurable return. ]^{ 95% and the
specific reason they cited was
integration.
>> Wow.
>> Getting the model to output text was
easy, but wiring it into the company's
actual nervous system that broke them.
>> I actually have to push back on this a
little bit.
>> go for it.
>> buy the cardboard cage analogy for
traditional software where you have to
like hardcode every single rule.
But LLMs already have the logic built
in.
>> Sure.
>> So if an AI can read and understand an
invoice,
why does it actually take months to make
it read a driver's log?
Isn't the whole point of AI that it
possesses a general capability?
>> See, you're touching on the exact trap
that catches really smart teams. The
capability is general, yes, but business
logic is not.
>> Ah, okay.
>> Stakeholders see a system handle one
document brilliantly. They recognize
that general intelligence and they
immediately demand general scope. They
want the tool to process every form in
the company.
>> Right, they want the magic bullet.
>> Exactly, but AI is a probabilistic
system, right? It's not a deterministic
one.
Every new document type introduces new
edge cases.
>> Oh, I see.
>> It introduces new compliance checks, new
validation rules, entirely new failure
states.
So yeah, the AI can read a driver's log
on day one,
but your overall system still has to be
coded to know what to actually do when
the AI inevitably hallucinates a
regulation.
>> Or when it just misinterprets a messy
handwritten note.
>> Exactly.
>> So the people who were your biggest
skeptics in week one suddenly become the
exact same people banging on your door
demanding these new general features in
week five.
>> Completely unaware of the engineering

>> And that shift from skepticism to just

accelerant for scope creep. I mean,
ordinary software projects already

>> Oh, yeah. The Project Management
Institute reports that 52%
