>> 52% And if you look at that joint
McKinsey
>> and Oxford study, the one that looked at
what, 5,400 IT projects?
>> Yeah, the massive one.
>> They found that large initiatives ran
45% over budget while delivering 56%
less value.
>> Which is just
staggering.
>> It is.
>> So AI is essentially throwing gasoline
on a fire that IT departments were
already struggling to put out.
>> Exactly.
And the data supports that entirely.
Futurum found that 46.9% of enterprises
overspent their AI budgets this year
alone.
>> This year alone.
>> Yeah. And nearly half of those companies
had to go back to leadership to ask for
more money.
They are fundamentally funding features
instead of funding outcomes.
>> So what does this mean for our baseline
then? If the gravity of AI naturally
pulls so strongly toward infinite
features and, you know, budget black
holes, what anchor do we use in our own
client work to keep these projects
grounded?
>> Well, we enforce an anchor that is
honestly almost embarrassingly simple.
It's just three components.
>> Okay, let's hear it.
>> One outcome, one owner, one date.
>> One outcome, one owner, one date. It
sounds like a motivational poster.
>> I know. I know it does. But I know from
our time in the trenches that it is
absolutely ruthless in practice.
>> it really is.
>> Let's look at the quoting team we work
with as a prime example of doing this
the right way.
When they started, they didn't set out
to build some vague AI for sales tool.
>> Or a comprehensive quote-to-cash
platform.
>> Right.
Their single outcome was defined with
almost microscopic precision. The
mandate was literally a draft quote for
every incoming request
reviewed by a human live in 6 weeks.
>> Nothing more, nothing less.
>> And naturally, once people saw it
successfully drafting quotes, what
happened?
The feature requests just started
pouring in.
>> Of course they did.
>> The sales team wanted live pricing
lookups. They wanted historical customer
data integrated.
>> But because they had that rigid anchor,
that one outcome, all of those requests
were deflected away from the current
build.
>> Yep.
They were placed onto a list for version
two. And because they held that line,
they actually hit their six-week date.
>> Which is huge.
>> They never hit backlog warning status.
And here's where it gets really
interesting.
Version two, which did include those
complex pricing lookups,
it ended up completely funding itself
from the return on investment generated
by the first win.
>> See, that's the dream. You start
generating real business value
immediately, which buys you the time and
the trust to build the next iteration.
>> Exactly.
>> You really have to contrast that
approach with a leader at a health
services company we spoke with recently.
>> Oh, right. I remember this.
>> Yeah, before his project even kicked
off, he told us point blank he would
rather pay for discovery up front than
build a massive unscoped system and find
out, in his words, we hate five out of
10 things.
>> He intuitively understood the risk of a
moving target. He knew that building a
massive wrong thing is infinitely worse
than building a small right thing.
>> Absolutely.
>> We actually had a developer on a
different drifting project tell us a
horror story that perfectly illustrates
the alternative.
>> Yeah, what did he say?
>> He told us that without a structured
request process and a firm scope, 90% of
their code base was just brittle
workarounds.
for things that should have been
specified before they wrote a single
line of code.
>> See, that's what happens. Creep forces
engineers to build in a constant state
of reaction. You aren't just adding
scope, you're adding the wrong scope.
>> Right.
>> And you're building it in a totally
unstable way just to accommodate
requirements that change, you know,
every Tuesday.
>> But and I have to play devil's advocate
here,
a rule on a whiteboard is just a wish
unless you have the mechanics to enforce
it.
>> That's true.
>> When a VP of sales demands a new feature
mid-sprint,
chanting one outcome, one owner, one
date isn't going to magically stop them.
>> No, it won't.
>> So how do we practically put this into
action?
>> Well, this is where we really rely on
our five practice checklist. This is the
actual operational system we use to run
our client engagements.
>> Okay, let's walk through it.
>> So So, one is simple but highly
effective. Write the not yet list on day
one.
>> Okay, but I imagine this causes some
friction, right? I mean, writing things
down sounds nice in theory,
but does a piece of paper really diffuse
a stakeholder who wants their idea built
right now?
>> It actually does, and it's because of
the psychology of sequencing.
>> Psychology of sequencing? What do you
mean?
>> Well, every single out-of-scope idea
gets written down on a visible list, and
it's explicitly tied to the name of the
person who requested it.
>> Huh.
>> And the thing is most of these are
genuinely brilliant ideas. So, when you
write it down next to their name, you
validate the stakeholder.
>> You're giving them credit.
>> Exactly. You absorb all the political
pressure in the room because nothing is

telling a VP no, you're telling them not

>> That makes a lot of sense.

of leads directly into the actual

Define done

metadata.title: The AI Scope-Creep Shield: How to Turn 'One More Request' into a Premium Change-Order That Pays Y...
metadata.author: Nomad Life Success
metadata.shortDescription: Every digital nomad knows the silent profit killer: scope creep. That 'quick tweak' after a project wraps, the 'small addition' that somehow takes three hours, the client who treats your retainer like an all-you-can-eat buffet. In this episode, Marcus Chen reveals how to build an AI-powered Scope-Creep Shield that catches these requests before they eat your income. You'll learn the exact prompt to classify incoming client messages as in-scope, out-of-scope, or expansion-worthy, and how to auto-generate a polished, premium-priced change-order in under two minutes. Marcus shares a simple three-tier pricing framework that turns annoying extras into your highest-margin work, plus the email script that makes clients thank you for charging more. You'll also hear the common mistakes nomads make when enforcing boundaries—like being too rigid—and how to avoid them. By the end, you'll have a repeatable system that protects your hourly rate, keeps clients happy, and creates more visa-qualifying income while you're sipping coffee in Chiang Mai. Stop working for free. Start building your shield today.

metadata.title: Stop AI Agent Scope Creep: Frozen Requirements and a Done When List
metadata.author: neomanex
metadata.shortDescription:
An agent drafts the requirements. I read every line, make the calls, and my yes freezes them. From then on, every step builds against that list, and only I can change it.

A piece that points at no requirement gets cut. What the plan won't do is written down. And every requirement gets a Done When box, so the plan has an end.

In this video I walk through a real plan, line by line: runners for AI agents, like GitLab runners, so a team can run our agents' jobs in its own cluster.

Start big: the initiative, with sixteen requirements, written for people
The split: its first plan took thirteen of them, and split them into thirty-six, row by row
Three parts on every line: who does it, what they can do, and how you'd prove it from the outside
Freeze it: an agent drafts the list, I make the calls, my yes freezes it
What it won't do, and a Done When box for every requirement
Every step reads the same list: the design, the rules, the tests, the last check
Round one: eight of twenty-five failed. Each failure got fixed, and tested again. Round five: thirty-six out of thirty-six
We teach this at Neomanex. Join Inside Neomanex, our network of builders, and we'll help you build your own: https://neomanex.com/join

Chapters 0:00 Requirements an agent can't misread 0:25 The job 0:41 Start big 1:26 The split 2:29 Three parts 3:32 Freeze it 4:11 What it won't do 4:44 Done When 5:12 Every step reads it 6:41 Round one 7:19 Back to the list 7:39 The method 8:43 Build your own

Tools in this video ConvOps (runs the workflows, the agents and the frozen requirements): https://convops.app

Neomanex: https://neomanex.com

metadata.title: How to Handle Scope Creep in Client Projects
metadata.author: WPTuts
metadata.shortDescription:
In this quick video, I address a common issue many face in client projects: scope creep. 

If you're unfamiliar with the term, scope creep occurs when clients request additional features or changes outside the initial project agreement. This can lead to more work and potential conflicts.

I share my approach to managing scope creep effectively by embracing client changes while protecting your time and resources. Key points include:

- This includes a section on changes and revisions in your project agreement.
- Being flexible but setting clear boundaries and cost implications for additional work.
- Using plain English contracts to make terms understandable for clients.

I also recommend the "Contract Killer" template, simplifying legal jargon and improving client understanding and conversion rates. Check out the link below for more details.

Uncapped Indemnity & Scope Creep: The Contract Traps Every Freelancer Faces

What starts as an innocent freelance gig can turn into financial ruin within weeks.

In this investigative documentary, "The Anatomy of a Freelance Catastrophe," we break down the silent traps hidden inside standard client agreements-from unchecked scope creep over informal WhatsApp messages to the ultimate legal landmine: uncapped indemnity clauses. Discover how these overlooked contractual obligations leave independent professionals vulnerable, and how AI-powered contract review tools like ClauseRadar are shifting the balance of power back to creators and freelancers.

Key Takeaways:

Why agreeing to "minor adjustments" without written change orders destroys margins.

What an uncapped indemnity clause actually means when third-party litigation hits.

How to negotiate liability caps tied strictly to your actual project fees.

The role of automated AI contract review in catching predatory legal clauses.

segments.text: A standard $4,000 contract lands in an
inbox. Two signatures later, the project
begins.
But months down the line, a single
clause buried in that paperwork can
trigger a $400,000 legal judgment
against the creator.
Independent contractors exist in a legal
blind spot.
Salaried employees have statutory safety
nets, minimum wage laws, workers'
compensation, and organized bargaining.
Freelancers operate outside of that
framework, covered entirely by the
private commercial contracts they sign.
When a client breaches those terms by
ignoring a $5,000 invoice, the only
recourse is civil litigation. Hiring a
lawyer and paying court fees to chase a
micro dispute quickly costs more than
the invoice is actually worth.
Without access to affordable dispute
resolution or basic labor protections,
independent workers operate in a
hazardous void, crossing their fingers
that the entities they work for will
behave ethically.
That reliance on goodwill forms the hope
and wish methodology of risk management.
Freelancers accept the work, deliver the
assets, and pray the project goes
smoothly.
Hope does not neutralize the two
specific factors that dismantle
independent businesses.
The first is behavioral manipulation,
and the second is predatory legal fine
print.
Both of these mechanisms extract value
by exploding a massive imbalance of
power.
On one side sits a corporate entity with
internal legal departments and financial
leverage. On the other, a solo operator
who needs to pay rent.
Operating blindly under these conditions
guarantees that eventually an asymmetric
risk will materialize and financially
break a freelance operation.
The bleed usually starts with the
proposal. When deliverables are listed
vaguely like website redesign instead of
six pages with two revision rounds,
clients interpret the agreement to
include as much output as possible.
When the client asks for more, the
platform power dynamic kicks in.
Freelancers rely heavily on public
ratings and client referrals to secure
their next job.
The threat of a one-star review
pressures them into quietly absorbing
the extra labor.
These scope expansions rarely arrive as
formal project amendments. They flow
through informal channels, texts and
direct messages disguised as one quick
favor or a minor final tweak.
This chart maps the mathematics of scope
creep. When a fixed fee two-week sprint
stretches into a five-week ordeal of
continuous revisions, the total
compensation remains identical while the
hours compound.
The effective hourly rate plummets
towards zero.
Stopping this requires a formalized
change order process.
When a boundary is crossed, work pauses
until the new request is quoted,
documented, and priced as an addition.
Without that pause, a technically
profitable project slowly morphs into a
system of voluntary unpaid labor.
While scope creep drains a business
slowly over text messages,
a fatal blow usually arrives fully
formatted in the contract's fine print.
The most dangerous clause in corporate
contracting is uncapped indemnification.
[snorts] It legally requires the
independent worker to pay for the
client's financial losses and legal
defense fees if a problem arises.
This flowchart illustrates the liability
chain.
Suppose a client provides an unlicensed
image or trademarked asset to a
freelance designer.
When the true owner of that asset, the
third party, sues the client for
copyright infringement,
the indemnity clause activates,
redirecting the weight of the
litigation.
The corporation legally forces the
isolated freelancer to pay the
exorbitant defense fees and damages,
even though the client supplied the
infringing material.
Surviving this exposure requires
negotiating an aggregate liability cap.
This specific wording limits the maximum
potential damages to the total dollar
amount actually paid to the contractor.
Signing an agreement without that cap
means accepting infinite ruinous
financial risk in exchange for a finite
minimal payout. Knowing these traps
exist and actually spotting them are two
different problems.
Hiring an attorney at hundreds of
dollars an hour to parse a $4,000
service agreement destroys the profit
margin before the work even begins.
Faced with this mathematical reality,
freelancers make a practical but
dangerous choice.
They sign complex binding legal
documents completely blind.
Corporate legal departments understand
this dynamic perfectly.
They draft aggressive agreements knowing
the individual contractor lacks the
resources to review them, passing all
enterprise risk down to the most
vulnerable party.
The traditional legal framework built on
expensive human counsel and prolonged
negotiation cannot scale to the volume
and velocity of the modern gig economy.
Bridging this gap requires an equalizer.
Platforms like Claus Radar deploy
automated risk detection, offering a
technological shield against predatory
drafting.
Instead of hours of expensive review,
algorithms scan service agreements in
seconds, exposing hidden landmines like
net 90 payment traps, early IP
handovers, and uncapped liabilities.
Pointing out a trap only solves half the
problem.
The software goes further by instantly
drafting precise plain English counter
proposals for every flagged clause.
These automated ready-to-send responses
give freelancers the exact phrasing
needed to push back and establish firm
legal boundaries without alienating
clients or destroying the relationship.
As freelance work evolves into a complex
ecosystem, relying on hope is a
mathematical error.
Utilizing automated precision offers the
only viable way for independent workers
to equalize structural leverage and
ensure their financial survival.

These automated ready-to-send responses give freelancers the exact phrasing needed to push back and establish firm legal boundaries without alienating clients or destroying the relationship. As freelance work evolves into a complex ecosystem, relying on hope is a mathematical error. Utilizing automated precision offers the only viable way for independent workers to equalize structural leverage and ensure their financial survival.

You'll learn how to scale cold email outreach, write cold emails that get replies, and use Claude AI to speed up cold emailing without burning your domains.

 If you're a founder or sales pro who wants to book more meetings, this AI cold email video is for you.

metadata.title: Cold Email is Dead — I Built an AI Outreach System That Does Everything for You (Lead to Meeting)
metadata.author: NoCode with Sam Oluwagbami
metadata.shortDescription:
Cold email and outbound sales are changing fast.

In this video, I break down how I built an AI-powered outbound sales automation system that handles the full outreach process automatically — from lead import to personalized emails, follow-ups, reply detection, and meeting booking.

This system (Outreach OS) is designed to help businesses scale outbound sales without manually sending emails or managing messy spreadsheets.

We cover:
- How to automate cold email outreach end-to-end
- AI-powered personalization for each lead
- Multi-step follow-up sequences
- How replies are detected and categorized automatically
- How meetings are booked without manual back-and-forth
- The simple stack behind a modern outbound system

This is not theory — it’s a working system that shows how SaaS-style outbound tools are actually built today using APIs, AI, and automation tools.

If you're interested in:
- AI sales automation
- outbound lead generation systems
- cold email tools
- SaaS MVP building
- no-code + AI workflows

This breakdown will show you exactly how it works under the hood.

#salesautomation #coldemailing #outbound #aiagents #saas  #leadgeneration #aiautomation #nocode #startups

metadata.author: Adam Holmgren
metadata.shortDescription:
Tired of hearing how great someone’s LinkedIn Ads strategy for B2B SaaS is… without ever seeing the actual campaigns?
Same.

That’s why I’m opening up our real ad account.

In this first episode of Inside an Ad Account, I walk through the exact LinkedIn Ads campaigns we used to go from 0 to 200 B2B SaaS customers at Fibbler.

You’ll see:
• How we structured the campaigns
• What targeting and creatives we used
• The KPIs that actually mattered
• Why some ads were shut off after just a few days

No fluff. No theory. Just the real campaigns that drove growth for Fibbler.

———

Subscribe for monthly deep dives into real ad accounts and interviews with some of the brightest LinkedIn Ads masterminds.

Learn more about Fibbler at fibbler.co.

#linkedinads #b2bmarketing #linkedinadsstrategy

1:05 Cold structure

8:06 Conversation Ads
9:16 Thought Leader Ads #2
10:30 Success metrics
11:07 Retargeting targeting
12:40 Influenced Attribution
13:06 Outro

Create content that attracts ICP interest and become a true authority in your category with LinkedIn content: https://compoundcontenttemplates.carrd.co/

I break down the exact linkedin lead generation system I’m using to win consistent, high-quality opportunities without cold spam. This linkedin marketing strategy is built for long-term results and works even as the platform evolves into 2026.

I explain how to design a scalable linkedin content strategy rooted in founder led content and strong personal branding linkedin, so the right people come to you. This approach is ideal for b2b lead generation, helping you generate predictable linkedin inbound leads using a proven linkedin 2026 strategy.

metadata.title: How to Get B2B Clients on LinkedIn in 2026 (Intent-Based Outreach System)
metadata.author: Jack
metadata.shortDescription:
Lazy B2B selling is dead. If you are still using the "spray and pray" approach for LinkedIn outreach and cold email, you are burning your pipeline.

In this video, Jack Hayes (CEO of Profit Jack Enterprises) breaks down the exact intent-based LinkedIn outreach system we use to generate high-ticket B2B leads for Fractional CMOs, Law Firms, and Marketing Agencies.

We pull back the curtain on our actual 2026 data: 31,000 connection requests sent, a 34% acceptance rate, and nearly 10,000 messages with a 26% reply rate. You'll learn how to use LinkedIn Sales Navigator to find active decision-makers, why we target new executives (in their role for less than a year), and how to build a B2B pipeline that runs while you sleep.

Whether you are a Fractional CMO looking for clients, or a B2B agency trying to scale, this is the outbound lead generation system you need.

👇 WORK WITH US:
Want us to build this exact intent-based outbound engine for your business?
Book a discovery call here: https://calendly.com/profitjack/thankyou

Get our complete B2B Outbound Playbook here: https://profitjack-dobs8cbb.manus.space/?code=Sn8fMEaF53ZwxgJGeqBSas

1:06 - Our 2026 LinkedIn Outreach Data (34% Acceptance Rate )
2:01 - How Intent-Based Outreach Actually Works
2:55 - The Best LinkedIn Sales Navigator Filters to Use
3:32 - Why You Must Target Active LinkedIn Users
4:08 - Real Client Results (Fractional CMOs & Agencies)

metadata.title: OpenAI's New Privacy Policy: What Every Business Owner Needs to Know
metadata.author: Micah Johnson
metadata.shortDescription:
OpenAI just released their brand new privacy policy and there are some major changes you need to be aware of. In this video, I break down everything that matters.

Whether you are a casual user, business owner, or enterprise customer, these privacy changes affect how your data is used, stored, and shared.

Note: This update applies to the US privacy policy only.

IMPORTANT SETTINGS:

Go to Settings, Data Controls, Toggle off Improve the model to opt out of training.

For Business Users:
If you are handling sensitive data, use the OpenAI API instead of the standard ChatGPT interface - your data is NOT used for training by default.

In this video:

- Training on your data: What's collected by default and how to turn it off
- API vs. ChatGPT consumer: The critical distinction for business owners
- New ad ecosystem: How free and Plus users are now part of personalized advertising
- Data collection expansion: Atlas browser, Sora uploads, and contact book access
- Enterprise account controls: What admins can see and access
- Deletion policies: Why "delete" doesn't always mean gone

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

TIMESTAMPS

0:00 - Intro
0:07 - Your data is training AI models (how to opt out)
0:37 - API vs ChatGPT: Critical difference for businesses
0:51 - Ads are here for free users
1:32 - New data collection (contacts, Sora, Atlas)
2:04 - "Delete" doesn't always mean gone
2:34 - Enterprise users: Your chats aren't private
3:05 - Data sharing & your rights
3:46 - Action steps for business owners

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

ABOUT THE CREATOR

I've built and exited multiple businesses, including a 125-employee company (2018 exit) and a mid-six-figure solo venture that taught me the hard way about the limits of going it alone. After working with hundreds of companies worldwide, I now teach founders to scale with AI automation and small, high-performing teams through cohorts and mastermind groups.

Connect with me:  https://linktr.ee/micah.bg
Check out my podcast:  https://automateyouragency.buzzsprout.com

metadata.title: Zero Data Retention Is Not Enough for AI Security (3 Controls Explained) #ai #aisecurity
metadata.author: Protecto
metadata.shortDescription:
Your AI provider says zero data retention. That doesn’t mean your data is safe. Zero data retention is only one of three separate controls, and none of them replaces the others.

Control 1, no training: your content isn’t used to train models. It says nothing about how long data is stored or where it’s processed.

Control 2, zero data retention: the provider doesn’t keep covered content after processing it. It doesn’t keep your data inside your environment or in a specific country, and it doesn’t cover your own logs, retrieval pipelines, or connected tools.

Control 3, data residency: where data is stored or processed. It doesn’t say whether data is used for training or how long it’s kept.

Provider settings vary by service, endpoint, and feature, so check each commitment against what your application actually uses. The model may be stateless, but your logs, retrieval pipeline, tools, and databases are not. The strongest safeguard is data minimization: the less sensitive data you send, the less you depend on a provider to protect it. This video covers the architecture difference between direct disclosure and a protection layer, and seven questions to ask before you trust a provider’s promise.

Book a demo: https://www.protecto.ai

Full breakdown: https://www.protecto.ai/blog/zero-data-retention-your-ai-model-may-be-stateless-your-system-isnt/

0:00 Zero data retention is not enough
0:17 The three controls
0:18 Control 1: No training
0:27 Control 2: Zero data retention
0:43 Control 3: Data residency
0:55 Three controls, three different questions
1:07 The model is stateless, your system isn’t
1:18 Data minimization: the strongest safeguard

1:48 Why agent workflows need this at every step
1:54 Questions to ask your provider
2:15 Control what you send first

metadata.title: OpenAI's Policies Explained: EU Privacy, Security, Safety, and Your Data Rights (ChatGPT, Sora,API)
metadata.author: Innovative Compass Consulting
metadata.shortDescription:
This video provides a deep dive into the official documentation from OpenAI regarding the practices governing their Services, including ChatGPT, DALL·E, Sora, and the API Platform. We break down the key commitments related to data collection, usage terms, security standards, and safety procedures.

🔍 Understanding Data Collection and Privacy
OpenAI collects several categories of Personal Data from users of its Services.
• Personal Data You Provide: This includes Account Information (name, contact details, payment information, transaction history) and User Content (your prompts, files, images, and audio uploads).
• Technical Information: When you use the Services, OpenAI receives Log Data (IP address, browser type, time of request), Usage Data (features used, content types viewed), and Device Information (operating system, device identifiers).
• Location Information: The general area from which your device accesses the Services is determined using information like the IP address for security reasons and to improve the product experience, or more precise GPS location if you choose to provide it.
How Data is Used: Personal Data is used to provide, analyze, and maintain the Services (e.g., responding to ChatGPT questions), improve and develop new features, communicate with users, prevent fraud or illegal activity, and comply with legal obligations. Content provided by users may be used to improve the Services, such as training the models that power ChatGPT, though users can opt out of this use.
Data Disclosure: Personal Data may be disclosed to vendors and service providers (like hosting services, payment processors, and customer service), affiliates, government authorities (if required by law), and parties involved in business transfers (Transactions). Note that if you join a ChatGPT Enterprise or business account, the administrators can access and control your account, including your Content.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
🛡️ Security, Compliance, and Safety
OpenAI is committed to building trust by protecting customer and user data, models, and products.
• Security & Compliance: OpenAI business products (API, ChatGPT Enterprise/Business/Edu) are covered by SOC 2 Type 2 and CSA STAR Level 1 reports, confirming controls align with industry standards for security and confidentiality. OpenAI supports customer compliance with privacy laws like GDPR and CCPA. They also invite security researchers to report issues through a Bug Bounty Program.
• Safety Approach: Safety involves an iterative process: Teach (filter data, follow policies, incorporate human values), Test (red teaming, system cards, preparedness evaluations), and Share (safety committees, feedback).
• Model Safety Evaluations: Comprehensive safety measures and evaluations are outlined in system cards for major models like GPT-5, Sora 2, GPT-4o, and OpenAI o3/o4-mini. These evaluations focus on risks like biological/chemical capability, cybersecurity, and AI self-improvement.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
📝 Key User Terms and Accuracy Warnings
When using services like ChatGPT and DALL·E, certain Terms of Use apply.
• Content Ownership: As between the user and OpenAI, users retain ownership rights in their Input and own the Output. OpenAI assigns all its right, title, and interest in and to the Output to the user.
• Accuracy Disclaimer: Users must understand that Output may not always be accurate due to the probabilistic nature of machine learning. Output should not be relied upon as a sole source of truth, factual information, or a substitute for professional advice. Users must evaluate Output for accuracy, using human review as appropriate, before using or sharing it.
• Mandatory Arbitration: Disputes arising out of or relating to the Terms or Services are generally resolved through final and binding mandatory arbitration with the National Arbitration and Mediation (“NAM”), though users may opt out within 30 days of account creation. Class arbitrations, class actions, and representative actions are prohibited.
• Cookies: OpenAI uses Necessary cookies (required for service functionality like user authentication and security), Analytics cookies (to understand service usage, often via Google Analytics), and Marketing Performance cookies (to measure campaign efficacy, often via LinkedIn, Google, Facebook, and TikTok). Necessary cookies cannot be disabled if you wish for the Services to function.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

metadata.title: Stop Sending Your Private Data to OpenAI's Servers
metadata.author: Matt Williams
metadata.shortDescription:
Did you know that your ChatGPT desktop conversations, uploaded files, and even snippets from your other open apps aren't just staying on your computer? By default, your most sensitive data, from proprietary source code to financial records, can be stored in the cloud and used to train future models.

In this video, I show you how to keep the seamless UI and shortcuts of the ChatGPT desktop app while swapping the "brain" for a local model using Ollama. This ensures your private data never leaves your hardware, giving you the power of AI without the privacy nightmare.

What you'll learn in this video:
- How to set up local models on your Mac.
- The "weird quirk" of the ChatGPT integration settings.
- Why "Opting Out" of training isn't enough to protect your privacy.
- How to verify that your AI is truly running offline.
- When to use cloud models vs. when to switch to local for maximum security.

metadata.title: AI Reads OpenAI's Privacy Policy, Finds Data Trap | WNT #lawyer #openai
metadata.author: WNT

segments.text: AI reads OpenAI's privacy policy, finds
data trap. OpenAI operates three
separate privacy frameworks depending on
where you live and how you access their
products, creating a fragmented
accountability structure that would make
any regulatory lawyer nervous. The EU
privacy policy updated in April 2024,
the general terms of service, and
separate FAQ documents for data controls
and memory features form a maze of
overlapping and sometimes contradictory
provisions. This isn't accidental. By
splitting key disclosures across
multiple documents, OpenAI ensures that
even the most diligent user will miss
crucial details about how their data
gets weaponized for model improvement.
The EU privacy policy contains a
particularly troubling section on
legitimate interests that functions as a
catch-all justification for data
processing.
OpenAI claims legitimate interest in
using your conversations to develop,
improve, and provide our services
without defining boundaries on what
improvement means or how long this
interest persists.
Under GDPR, General Data Protection
Regulation, Article 61F, companies can
process data based on legitimate
interests only when those interests
aren't overridden by individual privacy
rights. Open AAI never explains how they
balance this equation. They simply
assert the interest exists and move
forward. This vague framing opens the
door to indefinite data retention under
the guise of ongoing model development,
a practice that privacy regulators in
Ireland and the European data protection
board have started questioning. The data
controls FAQ reveals the real scope of
OpenAI's data ambitions through what it
doesn't say.
Users can supposedly turn off chat
history to prevent conversations from
appearing in their sidebar, but OpenAI
explicitly states that even with history
disabled, they retain conversations for
30 days to monitor for abuse before
deletion. Here's the slate of hand. That
30-day window gives OpenAI ample time to
extract, anonymize, and integrate your
prompts into training data sets before
the original chat technically gets
deleted. The FAQ mentions that disabling
chat history means conversations won't
be used to train our models, but
provides zero technical verification of
this claim. No audit trail, no
cryptographic proof, no third party
validation. You're supposed to trust
that OpenAI's internal systems properly
flag and exclude opted out conversations
from training pipelines. For a company
that routinely scrapes the entire
internet for training data, this
self-certification model lacks
credibility.
The memory FAQ introduces an even more
invasive feature that persists across
conversations. Chat GPT can now remember
details about you, your preferences, and
your life circumstances to provide more
relevant responses. OpenAI frames this
as user empowerment, but the technical
implementation reveals a permanent
profiling system. Memories are stored
indefinitely unless you manually delete
them. And OpenAI admits that memories
may be used to improve model performance
generally. Translation: Your personal
details become training data. The
company provides no granular controls
over what types of information chat GPT
can remember. You can't tell it to
remember work preferences, but forget
medical details.
It's all or nothing, and the default
setting is maximum retention. The policy
documents contain a stunning admission
about third-party sharing that most
users will never notice. OpenAI states
they may share personal data with
service providers and business partners
without naming these entities or
limiting the purposes of sharing. For EU
users, the policy references standard
contractual clauses for international
transfers, but doesn't disclose which
countries receive data or under what
security standards. The practical effect
is that your chat GPT conversations
could end up on servers in dozens of
jurisdictions with varying privacy
protections, and you have no right to
know which ones. This opacity violates
the spirit of GDPR's transparency
requirements, even if it technically
complies through dense legal language.
Critical loopholes emerge when comparing
stated policies against actual technical
capabilities. Open AAI claims anonymized
data can't identify individuals, but
research shows large language models can
memorize and regurgitate training
examples. Your supposedly anonymized
prompt could be reconstructed from model
outputs. The company reserves the right
to retain data as required by law
without specifying which laws or
jurisdictions trigger this retention.
This blank check could justify keeping
data indefinitely
for API application programming
interface business customers. OpenAI
promises not to use submitted data for
training unless explicitly permitted.
Consumer chat GPT users get no such
protection, creating a two-tiered
privacy system where enterprise clients
are valued and individuals are product.
The policies reference a data processing
addendum for business users, but provide
no equivalent protections for consumers
despite consumers generating the vast
majority of training data. OpenAI states
you can request data deletion under
GDPR, but the memory FAQ admits memories
may persist in model behavior even after
deletion. How can deletion be complete
if your information remains embedded in
model weights? The real genius of
OpenAI's policy construction is that it
places the burden of privacy protection
entirely on users while making effective
opt out nearly impossible.
Want to prevent your data from training
models? Disable chat history. Want to
stop memory collection? Turn off memory.
Want to avoid thirdparty sharing? Don't
use the service. But here's what they
don't tell you. Even with every privacy
toggle flipped, OpenAI still processes
your prompts to generate responses. And
that processing creates metadata, usage
patterns, and behavioral signals that
feed right back into model development.
The fine print acknowledges that
anonymized aggregate data remains fair
game regardless of your settings. Since
OpenAI defines what counts as
anonymized, they control the escape
hatch. The most legally vulnerable
aspect of these policies is the
fundamental misrepresentation of the
exchange. OpenAI presents chat GPT as a
service provided to users when the
economic reality is that users provide
training data as unpaid labor to OpenAI.
This inversion matters because consumer
protection laws globally require clear
disclosure when a transaction involves
non-monetary compensation.
If your prompts are payment for service,
then OpenAI's failure to quantify the
value of that data or offer alternatives
constitutes unfair business practice.
Class action attorneys in California,
where OpenAI is headquartered, could
argue that users are employees or
contractors entitled to compensation
under labor law. The policy documents
carefully avoid acknowledging this
relationship, describing data collection
as incidental rather than essential to
the business model.
That framing won't survive discovery in
litigation.

metadata.title: I Tested 5 AI Customer Support Chatbots — Ranked Worst to Best (2026)
metadata.author: AI Tool Lab
metadata.shortDescription:
One store inbox. Five AI support bots. Four of them will answer your customers — and only one of them will bill you fairly when they do.

I gave five AI support bots the SAME small online store inbox: a refund request, a "where is my order" question, a tricky policy question (worn once, 35 days later — still returnable?), and one trap message demanding 50% off or a chargeback with a fake order number. Then I ranked them worst to best on four scores: answer quality, honest pricing, setup effort, and what the free tier actually gives you.

CHAPTERS (real, from the final render):
0:00 Hook — five bots, only one bills fairly
0:35 The test — 4 scores, one inbox
1:29 #5 Zendesk AI — seats + meter, no free plan
2:31 #4 Gorgias — one answer, billed twice
3:27 #3 Intercom Fin — best answers, silence bills
4:30 #2 Chatbase — cheapest credit, 5x model tax
5:28 The twist — pause and guess: which bot bills a walkaway?
6:38 #1 Tidio Lyro — starts free, no seat stack
7:42 Outro — comment your pick

THE RANKING:
#5 Zendesk AI — the enterprise engine, and the worst deal here for a small store. Strong engine with clean handoffs, but the bill is a stack: Suite Team ~$55/agent/month billed annually, Copilot +$50/agent/month, then AI resolutions on top at ~$1.50 each committed ($2.00 pay-as-you-go) past a tiny $2/agent/month allowance. No free plan — 14-day trial only.
#4 Gorgias — the e-commerce native, and the one that bills you twice for a single answer. Order data inside the ticket makes it fastest on where-is-my-order, but each automated interaction (~$0.90 on annual plans, ~$1.50 past your bundle) ALSO counts as a helpdesk ticket. Plans from $10/month (50 tickets) to $50 (300 tickets). No free plan.
#3 Intercom Fin — the best answering bot here, and the one with the sneakiest definition of solved. Best refund and policy answers, calm no to the trap discount — but Fin bills $0.99 per outcome on top of seats from $29/month, and an outcome counts even when the customer simply goes quiet for 24 hours (an "assumed resolution"). Sales qualifications $9.99 each; standalone use carries a 50-outcome monthly minimum.
#2 Chatbase — nearly won on price alone, and the fastest bot to build here: paste your help pages and the widget is live the same afternoon. Free for 50 message credits/month, Hobby $40 for 700 credits, Standard $150 for 4,000 — but a credit is NOT an answer: one reply costs 1 credit on standard models but up to 5 on the strongest models, and action replies cost at least double. One AI agent per plan, no real helpdesk inbox on Hobby, and removing the Powered By badge costs $99/month more.
#1 Tidio Lyro — the best support bot here for a small store. Answers from your help content, plugs straight into Shopify, hands off to live chat in the same window. Honest catch: Lyro bills per conversation it joins, not per problem it solves. And the price is the friendliest here: a real free plan (50 conversations/month), Starter from $29/month, Lyro quotas from $39/month for 50 conversations (~$0.65 each billed annually) — but note the 50 free Lyro conversations are a one-time batch, not a monthly refill.

TOOL LINKS (official pricing pages — check the pricing page before you pay):
- Zendesk: https://www.zendesk.com/pricing
- Gorgias: https://www.gorgias.com/pricing
- Intercom Fin: https://www.intercom.com/pricing
- Chatbase: https://www.chatbase.co/pricing
- Tidio: https://www.tidio.com/pricing

PRICING DISCLAIMER: Prices change fast and several figures here are annual-billing or headline rates reported from Sept–Nov 2026 roundups (see seo-research.md for sources and flagged conflicts: Zendesk's old "Advanced AI" add-on was eliminated May 2026; Gorgias overage-rate sources differ; Chatbase plan names and Hobby credit counts vary by source; Tidio's "from $0.50/conversation" applies to sales-led tiers, self-serve runs $0.65–$0.78). Always check the tool's own pricing page before you pay. All demos in this video are simulated walkthroughs, not live screen captures, and no paid plan was bought for this video.

COMMENT YOUR PICK: Which of these five runs your store's inbox — the enterprise stack, the double meter, the silence counter, the credit meter, or the one that starts free? And when your last customer went quiet, did your bot solve it — or did it just bill you for the silence?

metadata.author: Ventra Technologies
metadata.shortDescription:
What if you didn't need to build the next ChatGPT to start an AI business?

Small businesses receive hundreds of repetitive customer questions every week — about orders, returns, pricing, delivery, bookings and more.

AI can now help automate a large part of that process.

In this video, we break down how an AI customer-support setup service works, what happens behind the scenes, and how you could turn this technology into a real service for small businesses.

What You'll Learn
Why businesses struggle with repetitive customer support
What an AI customer-support system actually does
Chatbots vs AI agents
How knowledge bases work
What RAG means in simple English
How AI connects with business software
How human handoff works
What APIs do behind the scenes
How to test and monitor an AI support system
How businesses can reduce repetitive support workload
How AI support can potentially influence revenue and retention
How you could package this into an AI service business
Real-World Examples

We'll look at examples involving companies such as Intercom, Zendesk, Shopify, Hospitable and Numan to understand how AI customer support is being used in real business environments.

Business Applications

The same principles can apply to:

E-commerce
Restaurants
Education businesses
SaaS companies
Service businesses
Appointment-based businesses
Online stores
Why This Matters

The future of AI isn't only about creating new AI models.

A major opportunity is helping existing businesses use AI to solve expensive, repetitive problems.

You don't necessarily need to build the technology from scratch.

You need to understand the problem, choose the right tools, connect the systems and make the workflow reliable.

Who Should Watch?

Students

segments.text: Imagine a local restaurant at 10:30 at
night. The doors are closed, but a
smartphone on the counter is vibrating
with dozens of WhatsApp messages.
Customers ask, "Are you open tomorrow?
Do you deliver here? And what is today's
special?" The owner is already home, but
tomorrow morning they will open their
phone and have to manually read, search
for the answers, and type out individual
replies to all of these identical
questions. Effectively, the business is
paying a human being to act as a slow
manual database, typing the exact same
information over and over again. This
flowchart shows the traditional customer
support loop and exactly where it
breaks. As customer volume increases,
the pathway from customer to message to
human exponentially multiplies until the
human node turns red and creates a total
bottleneck. The staff gets overwhelmed
and the customers are left waiting. This
bottleneck stems from the hundreds of
repetitive conversations that consume a
team's day, and solving it creates a
massive B2B service opportunity. A
business owner might think they can
solve this by simply plugging a raw AI
model directly into their website and
letting it talk to customers. But raw AI
models lack specific internal context.
Left unguided, they will hallucinate
return policies, invent prices, or
confidently provide outdated delivery
areas. A proper system requires a
knowledge base. This is an organized,
structured memory containing the
company's specific return windows,
menus, and logistics that the AI can
actually use. This abstract systems
model illustrates a concept called
retrieval augmented generation, or RAG.
When a customer asks a question, a
search beam scans the organized
knowledge base, extracts the specific
policy document, and feeds it into the
central AI processing node before it can
answer. Because the AI is forced to read
that extracted policy document first,
the text response emerging directly from
the node is accurate and tethered
directly to the business's actual rules.
High-quality, clearly structured
business data is the only thing that
makes an AI model useful for customer
support. Retrieving information is just
the first step. Modern AI agents can
also take autonomous action within a
business workflow. Looking back at our
processing node, we can see it extending
a connection line into a separate order
database. This is made possible through
APIs, application programming
interfaces. They allow the AI to
securely reach into external software,
retrieve a live tracking status, and
route it straight back to the user.
Giving software this level of access
requires strict guardrails. These are
explicit operating instructions
preventing the AI from promising
unauthorized refunds, guessing about
food allergies, or exposing private
customer data. The system must also be
designed with a human-in-the-loop

videos.full_text: Imagine a local restaurant at 10:30 at night. The doors are closed, but a smartphone on the counter is vibrating with dozens of WhatsApp messages. Customers ask, "Are you open tomorrow? Do you deliver here? And what is today's special?" The owner is already home, but tomorrow morning they will open their phone and have to manually read, search for the answers, and type out individual replies to all of these identical questions. Effectively, the business is paying a human being to act as a slow manual database, typing the exact same information over and over again. This flowchart shows the traditional customer support loop and exactly where it breaks. As customer volume increases, the pathway from customer to message to human exponentially multiplies until the human node turns red and creates a total bottleneck. The staff gets overwhelmed and the customers are left waiting. This bottleneck stems from the hundreds of repetitive conversations that consume a team's day, and solving it creates a massive B2B service opportunity. A business owner might think they can solve this by simply plugging a raw AI model directly into their website and letting it talk to customers. But raw AI models lack specific internal context. Left unguided, they will hallucinate return policies, invent prices, or confidently provide outdated delivery areas. A proper system requires a knowledge base. This is an organized, structured memory containing the company's specific return windows, menus, and logistics that the AI can actually use. This abstract systems model illustrates a concept called retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. When a customer asks a question, a search beam scans the organized knowledge base, extracts the specific policy document, and feeds it into the central AI processing node before it can answer. Because the AI is forced to read that extracted policy document first, the text response emerging directly from the node is accurate and tethered directly to the business's actual rules. High-quality, clearly structured business data is the only thing that makes an AI model useful for customer support. Retrieving information is just the first step. Modern AI agents can also take autonomous action within a business workflow. Looking back at our processing node, we can see it extending a connection line into a separate order database. This is made possible through APIs, application programming interfaces. They allow the AI to securely reach into external software, retrieve a live tracking status, and route it straight back to the user. Giving software this level of access requires strict guardrails. These are explicit operating instructions preventing the AI from promising unauthorized refunds, guessing about food allergies, or exposing private customer data. The system must also be designed with a human-in-the-loop safeguard. It constantly monitors the chat for complex, sensitive, or angry queries and immediately halts the automation when they occur. When the AI routes a frustrated to a human agent, it seamlessly passes along the full conversation history and the account details so the customer never has to repeat themselves. A successful implementation completely automates the routine tasks so that human employees are reserved strictly for high-stakes, sensitive interventions. Small business owners want these automated outcomes, but they rarely have the time or technical expertise to integrate APIs, set up RAG, and define guardrails themselves. That is where a specialized service provider comes in. The first phase of this offering is conducting a support audit, analyzing existing customer messages to identify exactly which repetitive questions can safely be automated. From there, the provider delivers a complete AI support setup package. This includes structuring the messy company data, configuring the agent's behavior, integrating the tools, and rigorously testing the human handoff protocols. A consultant's value comes from their grasp of niche operational workflows, like how a boutique clothing brand processes its returns versus how a clinic schedules appointments. The core product here is the recovery of human time and the boost in operational efficiency. This system replaces the chaotic manual late-night messaging loop with a unified support layer that manages multiple digital channels simultaneously. This line graph illustrates the primary financial benefit. Notice how the line representing customer volume rises steeply over time, while the second line representing support headcount remains completely flat. The business is absorbing massive increases in demand without a proportional increase in payroll. six is the rule that stops customers
from ever hating your automation. Step
one, list the 10 questions you answer
every single day.
Open your inbox, your WhatsApp, and your
comments, and write down the questions
that keep repeating. It is almost always
the same list. Where is my order? How
much is delivery? Can I return this? Do
you have this in stock? And what are
your opening hours?
If a question shows up three times a
week, it is a question your AI should be
answering, not you. 10 questions written
down is the foundation of everything
that follows. Step two, write the
answers once in one help document, and
make them honest and complete. For every
question on your list, write a short
answer with the real numbers, the
delivery time, the delivery cost, the
return window, and the refund rule.
Add your prices, your opening hours, and
your contact details.
This document becomes the brain of your
support system. If the answer is not
written down clearly, the AI will guess,
and a guessing AI is how a business
embarrasses itself in front of its own
customers. Step three, pick a support AI
tool that fits your size, not the
biggest one on the market. If you're a
small business, look at tools like
Intercom Fin, Zendesk AI, or Freshdesk
Freddy. And if you run your shop on
Shopify or WhatsApp, start with the AI
features already built into those
platforms.
The tool only needs to do three things:
read your help document, answer in your
tone, and hand over to a human when it
is stuck.
Most of them have a free
so test one for a week with your real
questions before you pay for anything.
Step four, set up instant answers for
the easy questions first, and do not try
to automate everything on day one.
Start with the five most common
questions from your list, the ones with
a fixed answer, like delivery times and
return rules.
Write each answer in plain words. Test
it by asking the question exactly the
way a customer would, and check that the
reply is correct, friendly, and short.
When those five work perfectly, add the
next five.
A support system that answers five
questions perfectly beats one that
answers 50 questions badly. Step five,
use AI to triage and route the hard
questions, so the right ones reach you
fast. Not every message is a simple
question. Some are complaints, some are
refund requests, and some are customers
ready to buy.
Set up your tool to tag each message,
urgent, refund, order problem, or ready
to buy.
The urgent ones and the buyers go to the
top of your list, and the routine ones
get an instant answer.
This one change can cut your response
time from hours to minutes, because you
stop digging through a messy inbox to
find the messages that matter. Step six,
the handover rule. And this is the step
most businesses skip. Never trap a
customer with a bot. Every automated
reply must offer a human in one tap. For
example, want me to get a person for
you? Just say human.
And set a clear rule. If the AI cannot
answer in two tries, it hands over
immediately with the whole conversation
attached, so the customer never has to
repeat themselves.
Customers do not hate AI support, they
hate being stuck with no way out. A fast
handover is what turns automation into
good service.
Step seven, measure it and fix the gaps
every week. Once a week, spend 20
minutes checking three numbers. How fast
the first reply went out, how many
questions the AI answered without a
human, and which questions it got wrong.
Take the top three questions it got
wrong, fix the answers in your help
document, and test them again.
That is it. Your support gets a little
smarter every single week. And after a
month, most of your routine questions
are handled before you even open your
inbox.
Now, the mistakes to avoid. First, do
not hide your phone number or your email
behind the bot because some customers
will always want a person and a hidden
contact loses sales.
Second, do not let the AI promise what
you cannot deliver like same-day
delivery you do not offer because a
broken promise costs more than a slow
reply.
Third, do not set it up once and never
check it because prices change, policies
change, and an old answer is worse than
no answer.
And fourth, do not automate the apology.
When a customer is upset, a human reply
is the only reply that works. Here's
your 7-day plan.
Day one, list your 10 most repeated
questions.
Day two, write the answers into one help
document.
Day three, pick a support AI tool and
start the free trial.
Day four, set up instant answers for
your five most common questions.
Day five, set up triage tags and the
human handover rule.
Day six, test it with 10 real customer
questions including a complaint and a
refund request.
Day seven, turn it on and watch your
first replies go out in seconds.
If this helped you, comment support
below and tell me the one question your
customers ask you most. Subscribe to AI
Wealth Path for daily AI and business
tips.
Learn AI tools, build smarter income. I
will see you in the next video.

segments.text: ﻿Hi everyone, this is Anna from Simply Contact - we make customer support simple.
Today, I’ll walk you through the Top 10 AI Customer Service Companies that are
shaping the future of customer support. We’ll look at what each company offers,
their key features, pricing, and what real users say about them.
Let’s get started. If you’re looking
for AI-powered outsourcing with real human support, let’s start with Simply Contact.
Simply Contact is a customer service outsourcing provider that
combines human agents with advanced AI tools. They use AI voicebots and chatbots, automated call
routing, and instant AI-powered translations. They also offer AI Quality Assurance and full
omnichannel support across calls, chats, and emails.
Pricing is customized based on project scope and support volume.
In practice, the results are strong. Simply Contact helped a European e-commerce
client reach a 94% customer satisfaction rate and reduce multilingual support costs.
They also launched a full government hotline in just one day.
If you want a reliable all-in-one support platform with strong automation,
Zendesk AI is a popular choice. Zendesk is one of the most widely
used support platforms in the world. Its AI suite includes chatbots, agent assistance,
automated ticketing, voice support, a knowledge base, and detailed analytics.
Pricing starts at 19 dollars per agent per month. Users often highlight Zendesk’s solid automation,
smooth workflows, and strong CRM integrations. For large and complex contact centers that need
deep analytics, NICE CXone stands out. NICE CXone is a cloud contact center
platform built around AI-driven workflows. Key features include real-time analytics,
omnichannel routing, AI automation, and powerful dashboards.
Digital agents start at 71 dollars per month, while voice agents begin at 94 dollars per month.
Users often mention how easy it is to track performance and manage large-scale operations.
If you’re looking for an AI agent that feels natural and fast, take a look at Fin by Intercom.
Fin handles automated chats, voice replies, and email responses.
It also supports human agents by pulling accurate answers directly from documentation.
Its main features include messaging automation, conversation analytics,
voice capabilities, and AI agent assist. Pricing starts with an entry-level AI plan,
with separate pricing for helpdesk features and an optional AI Copilot.
Users say Fin feels intuitive and delivers fast, accurate answers.
For teams focused on voice support and call automation, CloudTalk is a strong option.
CloudTalk is a cloud-based call center tool built around voice communication.
It offers smart call routing, call recording, real-time analytics, voice IVR, and AI tools
that guide agents during calls. Plans start at 25 euros per month,
with more advanced features in higher tiers. Customers appreciate CloudTalk for its simple
setup and easy CRM integrations. If you’re a small or mid-sized
business looking for an affordable AI chatbot combined with live chat, Tidio is a good fit.
Tidio combines AI chatbots, live chat, and helpdesk tools in one platform.
Key features include an AI assistant, custom automation flows, and built-in ticketing.
Pricing is flexible, with entry-level plans and advanced options for larger businesses.
Users often mention quick setup, a flexible flow builder, and reliable automation.
If your goal is to automate support and pay only for results, CoSupport AI is worth considering.
CoSupport AI focuses on full automation and uses a pay-per-resolution model.
It includes an AI agent for customer inquiries, an assistant for human agents, multilingual support,
and advanced analytics. Pricing is performance-based,
with a cost per resolved case and an additional monthly platform fee.
Users report around 40% faster response times and up to 68% ticket deflection.
For voice analytics and improving agent performance, Observe AI leads the category.
Observe AI specializes in voice analysis and AI-powered quality assurance.
Its features include AI voice agents, real-time agent coaching, automated QA
scoring, and full call and screen recording. Pricing follows a pay-per-request model.
Users value its accurate conversation analysis and practical coaching insights.
If messaging is your main support channel,
LivePerson is one of the strongest platforms available.
LivePerson focuses on conversational AI for automated digital messaging.
It offers generative AI tools, sentiment and intent analysis,
conversational automation, and many integrations. Pricing is customized based on business needs.
Users highlight time savings, strong sentiment tracking,
and the ability to handle high message volumes. For real-time agent coaching and on-the-spot
guidance, Cresta is a standout solution. Cresta supports agents during live conversations
with real-time suggestions and coaching. Its features include conversation intelligence,
automated quality insights, and performance analytics.
Pricing is custom and based on usage. Users appreciate the real-time support that
boosts agent confidence and improves both support and sales results.
So these were the Top 10 AI Customer Service Companies to know in 2025.
Each solution has its own strengths — from full automation,
to deep analytics, to real-time coaching. When choosing a platform, focus on what
matters most for your team: automation, voice support, messaging, or performance insights.
You can find more details in the article linked in the description.
Make sure to follow us for more content on CX and customer support. Bye for now!

If you’re looking for AI-powered outsourcing with real human support, let’s start with Simply Contact. Simply Contact is a customer service outsourcing provider that combines human agents with advanced AI tools. They use AI voicebots and chatbots, automated call routing, and instant AI-powered translations. They also offer AI Quality Assurance and full omnichannel support across calls, chats, and emails. Pricing is customized based on project scope and support volume. In practice, the results are strong. Simply Contact helped a European e-commerce client reach a 94% customer satisfaction rate and reduce multilingual support costs. They also launched a full government hotline in just one day. If you want a reliable all-in-one support platform with strong automation, Zendesk AI is a popular choice. Zendesk is one of the most widely used support platforms in the world. Its AI suite includes chatbots, agent assistance, automated ticketing, voice support, a knowledge base, and detailed analytics. Pricing starts at 19 dollars per agent per month. Users often highlight Zendesk’s solid automation, smooth workflows, and strong CRM integrations. For large and complex contact centers that need deep analytics, NICE CXone stands out. NICE CXone is a cloud contact center platform built around AI-driven workflows. Key features include real-time analytics, omnichannel routing, AI automation, and powerful dashboards. Digital agents start at 71 dollars per month, while voice agents begin at 94 dollars per month. Users often mention how easy it is to track performance and manage large-scale operations. If you’re looking for an AI agent that feels natural and fast, take a look at Fin by Intercom. Fin handles automated chats, voice replies, and email responses. It also supports human agents by pulling accurate answers directly from documentation. Its main features include messaging automation, conversation analytics, voice capabilities, and AI agent assist. Pricing starts with an entry-level AI plan, with separate pricing for helpdesk features and an optional AI Copilot. Users say Fin feels intuitive and delivers fast, accurate answers. For teams focused on voice support and call automation, CloudTalk is a strong option. CloudTalk is a cloud-based call center tool built around voice communication. It offers smart call routing, call recording, real-time analytics, voice IVR, and AI tools that guide agents during calls. Plans start at 25 euros per month, with more advanced features in higher tiers. Customers appreciate CloudTalk for its simple setup and easy CRM integrations. If you’re a small or mid-sized business looking for an affordable AI chatbot combined with live chat, Tidio is a good fit. Tidio combines AI chatbots, live chat, and helpdesk tools in one platform. Key features include an AI assistant, custom automation flows, and built-in ticketing. Pricing is flexible, with entry-level plans and advanced options for larger businesses. Users often mention quick setup, a flexible flow builder, and reliable automation. If your goal is to automate support and pay only for results, CoSupport AI is worth considering. CoSupport AI focuses on full automation and uses a pay-per-resolution model. It includes an AI agent for customer inquiries, an assistant for human agents, multilingual support, and advanced analytics. Pricing is performance-based, with a cost per resolved case and an additional monthly platform fee. Users report around 40% faster response times and up to 68% ticket deflection. For voice analytics and improving agent performance, Observe AI leads the category. Observe AI specializes in voice analysis and AI-powered quality assurance. Its features include AI voice agents, real-time agent coaching, automated QA scoring, and full call and screen recording. Pricing follows a pay-per-request model. Users value its accurate conversation analysis and practical coaching insights. If messaging is your main support channel, LivePerson is one of the strongest platforms available. LivePerson focuses on conversational AI for automated digital messaging. It offers generative AI tools, sentiment and intent analysis, conversational automation, and many integrations. Pricing is customized based on business needs. Users highlight time savings, strong sentiment tracking, and the ability to handle high message volumes. For real-time agent coaching and on-the-spot guidance, Cresta is a standout solution. Cresta supports agents during live conversations with real-time suggestions and coaching. Its features include conversation intelligence, automated quality insights, and performance analytics. Pricing is custom and based on usage. Users appreciate the real-time support that boosts agent confidence and improves both support and sales results. So these were the Top 10 AI Customer Service Companies to know in 2025. Each solution has its own strengths — from full automation, to deep analytics, to real-time coaching. When choosing a platform, focus on what matters most for your team: automation, voice support, messaging, or performance insights. You can find more details in the article linked in the description. metadata.title: How Much Should a Small Business Budget for AI Customer Support in 2026?
metadata.author: Rocket Research
metadata.shortDescription: In 2026, budgeting for AI customer support in a small business depends on factors like team size, usage volume, and pricing models. We explore the pricing structures of popular AI customer support platforms such as Corebee, Intercom, Zendesk, Gorgias, and Tidio to give you a clear picture of what to expect. Corebee offers a flat monthly rate with unlimited AI conversations and teammates, while Intercom and Zendesk combine per-agent fees with usage-based charges for AI outcomes. How do monthly costs vary between per-seat plus per-resolution pricing and flat-rate plans? What are the typical minimum commitments and usage fees? How do implementation and volume caps affect your budget? This video covers these questions and compares pricing details from top vendors like Corebee, Intercom, Zendesk, Gorgias, Tidio, and others to help you plan your 2026 AI customer support budget effectively. Watch to learn about the different pricing models and what small businesses can expect to pay for AI chatbots and helpdesk automation this year. This video discusses Chatwoot, DelightChat, Help Scout, and Crisp.

segments.text: In 2026, small businesses budgeting for
AI customer support should expect a
range of pricing models that combine
seat-based fees with usage charges or
offer flat monthly rates with no per
resolution fees. We evaluated several
leading options including Corby,
Intercom, Zenesk, Gorgeous, and Tidio.
To understand the cost involved, Corby
provides a straightforward pricing model
with a flat monthly fee starting at $99
for the pro plan. This includes
unlimited AI conversations, unlimited
teammates, and no per resolution fees.
This means your costs remain predictable
whether your team grows or your AI
handles more customer interactions.
Corby also offers a free tier with 50 AI
conversations monthly and a 14-day prot
trial. Intercom's pricing combines seat
fees starting at $29 per agent per month
with their Fing AI agent priced at 99
cents per outcome. An outcome refers to
any resolved conversation or handoff
with a minimum monthly commitment often
around 50 outcomes. Annual billing
lowers the seat price to $29 compared to
$39 monthly. Their advanced plans can go
up to $132 per seat monthly. This model
means costs scale with both team size
and usage volume. Zenesk offers annual
plans starting at $19 per agent per
month with monthly rates higher at $25.
AI agents are included in suite and
support plans, but come with usage based
fees of about $1.50 to $2 per automated
resolution. Additional AI features like
Copilot add about $50 per agent monthly.
This combination of seat and per
resolution pricing can increase costs
quickly for growing teams with high AI
usage. Gorgeous, popular among Shopify
merchants, charges AI agent fees around
90 cents to a dollar per resolved
conversation with base plans starting at
$59 monthly flat for up to 500 responded
conversations. Overages apply beyond
included limits, making budgeting
dependent on ticket volume. Tidio offers
starter plans from $29 monthly with 100
billable conversations, scaling up with
higher tiers. Their AI add-on, Lyro,
starts at $32.50 per month for 50
conversations. Ticket caps and
conversation limits mean costs can rise
with usage. Other vendors like Chatwoot,
Delight Chat, Help Scout, and Crisp use
various combinations of per agent fees,
AI credit meters, and conversation caps.
For example, Chatwoot charges $19 to $99
per agent monthly, plus AI credit
bundles that scale with usage, while
Help Scout adds 75 cents per AI
resolution on top of user fees. In
summary, small businesses in 2026 should
budget based on their expected team size
and AI conversation volume. Flat rate
plans like Corby's $99 monthly offer
predictable costs without per resolution
fees or seat charges. In contrast,
platforms like Intercom and Zenesk
combine seat fees starting around $19 to
$29 with per outcome charges near $1
each, which can add up as usage grows.
Consider whether your business prefers
capped or uncapped AI conversations,
fixed or usage based pricing, and how
many agents will use the system. This
overview helps clarify what small
businesses should expect to pay for AI
customer support software and chat bots
in 2026, allowing for better financial
planning and vendor selection.

Number one, Intercom, the AI first help desk and home to Finn, the smartest AI agent on this list. Intercom is live chat, a shared inbox, a help center, and ticketing across chat, email, phone, WhatsApp, SMS, social, and Slack. Finn is its AI agent. It answers customers on its own in your brand voice, and Intercom says it resolves about 76% of conversations without a human touching them. There's also Finn Copilot, which sits beside your human agents and suggests replies and summaries at $29 per agent a month. Now the pricing and the trap. Essential starts around $29 per seat a month, billed yearly. Advanced is around $85 per seat, and expert around 132. But Finn is billed separately on every plan. 99 cents per successful outcome every time Finn actually solves a conversation. The seat price does not cover it. There's no free plan, just a 14-day free trial, no credit card required. A real example. A bike shop in Austin gets 200 customer chats a month. Finn resolves 150 of them. That is about $150 in Finn fees on top of the $29 seat. If you want the highest resolution AI agent out there and you're happy paying solved chat, start here. Early stage startups can also get up to 93% off in year one through Intercom's early stage program. Worth checking if you qualify. Number two, Zendesk. The big name suite, the one most US companies already know. It does email ticketing, live chat, voice, a help center, and every channel in one place. Its AI agents handle generative replies and simple resolutions, and Copilot assists your agents. But Copilot costs $50 per agent a month and only on Suite Professional and above. Here is the trap, and it is a double one. First, there is no free plan, just a 14 day trial. Second, the cheapest plan, Support Team at around $19 per agent a month, is email ticketing only. No live chat and no AI agents. The real starting point for AI is Suite Team from around $55 per agent a month billed yearly. Suite Professional is from around $115 per agent a month. And even then, the AI agents include only a tiny allowance, five resolutions per agent a month on Team, 10 on Professional. And after that, you pay roughly $1.50 to $2 per automated resolution. Zendesk does not even publish the overage rate clearly. So a three person team on Suite Team is already paying about $165 a month before a single AI resolution over the allowance. If you want the safe big brand pick with live supported scale, Zendesk is solid. But it is not built for a one or two person team, and the AI bill sits on top of the seat bill. Number three, Tidio, the budget pick and the one built for small online stores. It is live chat, ticketing, email, messenger, Instagram, and WhatsApp in one inbox, and it plugs straight into Shopify, WooCommerce, and WordPress. Its AI agent is called Lyro, and it answers chats on its own. Copilot helps your write replies and flows are no code automations. Now the pricing and the third trap. Tidio has the most generous free start here. A free plan with 50 billable conversations a month, 10 seats, live chat, and ticketing. Starter starts around $29 a month for 100 conversations. Growth starts around $59 a month. But here's the Lyro trap. The 50 free Lyro conversations are a one-off lifetime grant, not monthly. To keep Lyro running, you buy a Lyro package separately from around $39 a month for 50 AI conversations. So starter at $29 a month does not mean unlimited Lyro. The real cost of an AI agent on Tidio is starter plus Lyro, about $68 a month combined. That is still the cheapest AI agent on this list, and it is the only one of the three you can start using for free today. If you run a small online store and want to start free, this is your pick. So how do you choose? It comes down to how each tool charges for its AI. Intercom charges 99 cents per resolved outcome. Zendesk charges roughly $1.50 to $2 per resolution after a tiny allowance. Tidio charges a flat $39 a month for 50 Lyro conversations. For a free start, Tidio wins easily. A real free plan against two 14-day trials. For AI on a budget, Tidio starter plus Lyro at about $68 a month is the cheapest way to have an AI agent answering. Intercom Essential plus Fin outcomes is $29 per seat plus 99 cents each. And for a shop getting 150 resolved chats a month, that is already about $180. Zendesk Suite team is $55 per agent before any AI overage, so it is the most expensive of the three for a small team. My rule of thumb, pick Tidio if you run a small online store and want to start free. Pick Intercom if you want the highest resolution AI agent and you will pay per outcome. Pick Zendesk if you want the big brand suite and live support at scale, not for a one or two person team. And whatever you pick, use the free plan or the free trial for two weeks and track two numbers. How many chats the AI resolves on its own and what that costs you per resolution. If the AI is saving you an hour a day, keep it. If not, try the next one. And remember, prices change, so check the vendor's site before you buy. metadata.shortDescription:
Your CRM might have thousands of contacts, but how many of them have complete and updated information?

In this video, we solve one of the most common problems sales teams face: incomplete and outdated CRM data.

Using Claude Code, MoltSets, and HubSpot, we demonstrate how to automatically identify missing information, enrich contact records, verify email addresses, detect potential job changes, and update everything directly inside your CRM without manually exporting or importing CSV files.

What we cover:

- Connecting HubSpot CRM with Claude Code
- Using the MoltSets Bulk List Enrichment Skill
- Enriching missing contact and company information
- Email verification and identifying potential job changes
- Managing enrichment credits and reviewing results
- Automatically updating enriched data in HubSpot
- Exploring PhantomBuster as an alternative

The goal is simple: keep your CRM data accurate, enriched, and ready for sales outreach.

MoltSets Skill: https://moltsets.com/library/skills/hubspot-bulk-list-enrichment/

Subscribe for more practical GTM Engineering, AI automation, and sales workflow tutorials.

#ClaudeCode #HubSpot #CRMEnrichment #MoltSets #GTMEngineering #SalesAutomation

metadata.title: Revolutionize Your Sales: Automated AI Prospecting with HubSpot & Clay
metadata.author: RevPartners - RevOps + GTM Engineering on HubSpot
metadata.shortDescription:
Stop wasting hours on manual research and outdated databases. This video reveals the "AllBound" orchestration framework, showing you how to combine HubSpot CRM with Clay’s AI power to automate deep account research, source verified ICP contacts, and trigger outreach based on real-time buying signals. Learn how to transition from cold, volume-driven activity to frictionless, conversion-driven prospecting that empowers your sales team to focus on high-value interactions.

#SalesAutomation #AIProspecting #HubSpot #Clay #LeadGeneration #B2BMarketing #RevenueOperations #SalesEfficiency #GTMStrategy #salesenablement

Poor reporting, inefficient workflows, and wasted time for your entire team.

At Sculpted, we use Clay, our custom integration layer, and deep go-to-market expertise to clean and enrich CRM data in a way no other solution can. We’ve helped companies like TrackSuit transform their CRM with highly accurate, actionable data that drives real business impact.
