metadata.title: Don't Start An AI Automation Agency. Build This Instead.
metadata.author: Alex Andreessen
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to work with me 1-on-1 to AI-enable and scale your agency? Click here: https://alexandreessen.com/haa/?utm_source=yt&utm_medium=aioutreach

________________________________________________

AAA is the new SMMA-of-2022: tons of hype, tons of course sellers, very little real business underneath. The systems you build for clients today are obsolete in 6 months, and that's not a business, it's a treadmill. I'm saying this as someone running a 7-figure paid ads agency with AI in every part of the operation, so this isn't an anti-AI take. In this video I break down the AAA hype cycle, the structural reasons it's a trap, why a marketing agency is the most durable model there is, and exactly how I run a $200k/mo agency with AI as the layer underneath, not the product on top.

________________________________________________

If you‘re new here, my name is Alex. I‘m 21 years old, from Norway, and I run a 100k+/month AI-enabled marketing agency called Curve. I started the agency in August 2023, but I have been hustling since I was 12.

This is how I got here:

2017 (12yo): Got my first laptop and got addicted to Minecraft and Photoshop.
2018 (13yo): Began freelancing making graphic design for Minecraft servers.
2019 (14yo): Started my own Minecraft server while doing graphic design on the side.
2020 (15yo): Poured 2 years of my life and 2k+ of my savings into the Minecraft server, before finally shutting it down.
2022 (16yo): Started Designr, my first agency, offering subscription-based graphic design services.
2023 (18yo): Transitioned from graphic design to paid advertising and started Curve.
January 2024 (18yo): First 10k month
July 2024 (19yo): First 50k month
January 2025 (19yo): First 75k month
April 2025 (20yo): First 100k month
June 2026 (21yo): First 200k month

As you can see, I‘m no wonder kid. I don‘t come from an ultra wealthy family and I have done my fair share of stumbling and falling in business.

With that being said, I believe that what I achieved could have been done A LOT faster if I had the right information, and the goal with this channel is to give you that information.

Wanna join me for the ride?

________________________________________________

Follow me on IG: @alexandreessen

agencies. Each business model makes the
first movers a ton of money while
everyone else gets crushed and AI
automation agency will be no different.
I'm saying this as someone actively
running a seven-figure a year paid ads
agency with AI integrated in every part
of the operation. I'm not anti-AI. I'm
anti-building a business on a trend. So,
why do I believe that an AI automation
agency is such a model? Well, it
creates five traps. So, let me run
through each one quickly. Trap number
one is that the AI industry is
innovating so quickly and completely
rebuilding the tools you have at your
disposal every three to six months. In
early 2024 custom GPTs were the moat.
Agencies were charging 5K to build them.
Then in 2025 Manas was the new shiny
object but then it came and went in like
a quarter. In early 2026 Open Claw was
the You probably saw it everywhere
on your feed. Suddenly they the bed
in terms of data safety. It was too
difficult and unpredictable to use and
everyone switched away. Point is,
whatever is hot today will be obsolete
by autumn. Picture this from a client's
perspective. You sold them an Open Claw
built in January then you come back in
April and you say, "Remember that AI
system I built you? Well, it's
compromised. I have to rebuild it on a
different platform so pay me again."
That's the AI automation hamster wheel.
It's a constant rebuild cycle. Trap
number two is that any successful agency
that does over seven figures a year runs
on MRR while AI automation agencies run
on one-time packages. Let's say you
charge 3 to 5K for a workflow, deliver
it and then what? You're back to just
selling new clients next month and the
month after in perpetuity. I know that
some agencies try to then upsell like a
$7 to $900 a month maintenance fee, but
why would the client pay you to maintain
something that works? The whole idea
with building AI systems is that they
reduce the dependence on people and
increase your margin. So, the harsh math
is that if you charge 5K per build and
want to hit, let's say, 30K a month,
which still isn't really, you have
to close six new clients every single
month permanently. At that point, you're
just freelancing and not really building
an actual business. And now compare that
to a paid ads agency. For example, a
client signs a 6K a month retainer and
stays with you for 9 months on average,
and these aren't made up numbers, by the
way. It's literally what my agency looks
like. In this scenario, you have a
LTV from one client. An AI automation
agency needs 10 clients to match that.
Trap number three is that an AI
automation agency doesn't actually own
anything. Your whole offer is wrapped
around someone else's API. Look at what
happened on the 4th of April this year.
I was doubling in Open Claude myself
until Claude banned using your existing
Claude Max subscription to run your Open
Claude agent. So, my costs literally
10x'd in a single month. Instead of
paying $200 a month for the
subscription, I burned through two grand
in tokens in a few weeks until I shut it
down. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic
are constantly launching new features
that make these custom agentic workflows
obsolete. You can now, for example, chat
with your Claude code project through
Telegram, which was a huge selling point
for Open Claude. Thing is, real
businesses have what is called a moat, a
competitive advantage, like
relationships, a brand, a compounding
skill. An AI automation agency has none
of that. You're basically a thin service
layer between a billion-dollar AI
company and the customer, and both ends
can squeeze you out whenever they want
to. Trap number four is that your
pricing collapses every 12 months. The
AI build-out that costs 5K today will be
a $19 a month SaaS feature tomorrow
because chances are what you're building

number five is the exit value. Try

year
at 60% net margin. So I can exit my

So I'm not only making $75,000 a month

paper for now. This may not bother you

metadata.title: 13 Businesses for the Age of AI
metadata.author: Greg Isenberg
metadata.shortDescription:
In this solo episode, I walk through the 13 businesses I think are left to build in the agentic era. I believe that in a world of agents and abundance, owning the right assets puts you in a better position. For each business, I explain what it is, why it holds up in a world of agents, and one or two examples, from Othership's sauna clubs to Osmo's window-cleaning robots. This episode gives you a map of where to build next, at any age.

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
01:15 – AI-Native Service Firms
02:57 – Offline Businesses
05:41 – Distribution and Organic Audiences
07:34 – Proprietary Data Sets
09:08 – Domain-Specific Harnesses
12:16 – Robotics and Physical AI
14:01 – Physical Products With a Fan Following
16:34 – Compute and Energy
17:31 – Health, Longevity, and Care
19:30 – Marketplaces and Social Networks
21:04 – Real Assets
21:46 – Vertical Agents
22:18 – Security
24:08 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• In an AI-native service firm, agents do most of the delivery and a human reviews the exceptions.
• Ad clicks went from about five cents in 2009 to $1–5 today, so I start with organic audiences.
• Proprietary data and domain-specific harnesses are the two gold rushes I see right now.
• Offline businesses, niche hardware, and robotics sell rooms, objects, and labor that agents only support.
• Compute, energy, and security are the scarce inputs every agent depends on.

metadata.shortDescription:
Build Free AI Agents & Workflow Automation With Zero Zapier Fees (Self-Hosted n8n + Free Groq/Gemini APIs)

Replace $50/mo Zapier & n8n Cloud Pro plans by self-hosting n8n Community Edition (211K+ GitHub stars, 400+ integrations, native MCP AI Agents) with Docker Compose and connecting free Groq (500+ tok/s), Google Gemini 2.5 Flash, or local Ollama models—with zero monthly execution limits.

📋 Complete Copy-Paste Hardened docker-compose.yml:
```yaml
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:2.48.7
    container_name: n8n-ai-agents
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"   # Open http://localhost:5678
    environment:
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=UTC
      - N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY}
      - WEBHOOK_URL=https://n8n.yourdomain.com/
      - N8N_SECURE_COOKIE=true
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true
      - EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE=168   # Keep 7 days
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n      # Persists workflows!
    restart: unless-stopped
volumes:
  n8n_data:
```

🔑 Generate Persistent Encryption Key (.env):
echo "N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"  .env

metadata.title: The Art of Solo Success: Building a Million-Dollar Design Empire from Scratch
metadata.author: Design Pickle
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Jar of Genius, host Russ Perry is joined by Brett Williams, Founder of Designjoy. Together, they unpack the secrets behind building a successful solo venture, the challenges of innovating within a saturated market, and the future of design entrepreneurship. Discover how Brett combined the benefits of traditional agencies and freelancing to create a one-man agency that offers affordable and reliable design services, as well as the impact of AI on the creative industry.



As the Founder of Designjoy, Brett operates a successful one-man design agency that generates $100k monthly. Pioneering the productized service model, he was the first to offer web design and branding on a subscription basis in 2017. Brett is also a freelance Senior UX/UI Designer. Previously, he co-founded Babblr, where he led the Design and Marketing teams. Brett's transition from a traditional graphic design role to creating a million-dollar business showcases the powerful combination of creativity and entrepreneurship.



If you enjoyed this episode, make sure to subscribe, rate and review on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and Google Podcasts, instructions on how to do this are here (https://www.fame.so/follow-rate-review) .



Previous guests include: Dan Martell of SAAS Academy (https://www.linkedin.com/in/dmartell/) , Chris Ronzio of Trainual (https://www.linkedin.com/in/chrisronzio/) , Jason Fried of Basecamp (https://www.linkedin.com/in/jason-fried/) , Julia McCoy of Content at Scale (https://www.linkedin.com/in/juliaemccoy/) , and Rob Morris of Design Pickle (https://www.linkedin.com/in/robertmorris72/) .
